lib.finfet.name: FinFET transistor
lib.finfet.blurb: The switch everything is made of. A voltage on the gate decides whether current flows: at 0 V the path along the fin is shut; at the supply rail (0.517 V on a minion) the gate's field pulls a thin sheet of electrons into the fin, and current flows from source to drain. The gate drapes over the fins on three sides.

lib.fin.name: The fin, in section
lib.fin.blurb: A wall of crystalline silicon 6 nm thick and 52 nm tall, tapered with a rounded top; fins stand 30 nm apart. The gate wraps over three sides, so it holds the channel shut tightly: that is why fins replaced flat transistors.
lib.fin.note: N7's fin: 6 nm wide and 52 nm tall (WikiChip Fuse on TSMC's IEDM 2016 paper); the earlier drawing's 6-7 by 45-50 nm, inferred from 10 nm-class sections, is superseded

lib.gate.name: Gate stack
lib.gate.blurb: The gate: a metal electrode on an insulating layer only a few atoms thick (hafnium oxide on a thin silicon oxide), wrapped over the top and both sides of the fin. Its metal's work function sets the voltage at which the transistor turns on.
lib.gate.note: effective gate length about 16.5 nm (N7, Dick James on IEDM 2016); the earlier 20 nm (IRDS, 7 nm-class) is superseded

lib.channel.name: Channel (the silicon under the gate)
lib.channel.blurb: The strip of fin under the gate, 16.5 nm long, where the current flows: about 257,000 silicon atoms and almost no dopant atoms. Off, it is nearly empty of free electrons; on, the gate pulls in about a hundred.
lib.channel.note: the channel's length, the effective gate length of N7: 16.5 nm; the channel is 6 nm wide and 52 nm tall

lib.si.name: Silicon crystal
lib.si.blurb: Silicon atoms in a diamond lattice, each bonded to four neighbours. Every outer electron is held in a bond; freeing one takes 1.12 eV, 43 times the thermal energy at room temperature, so pure silicon barely conducts. A transistor's electrons come from its doped source instead.

lib.dramcell.name: A DRAM cell, in section
lib.dramcell.blurb: A DRAM bit is charge on one tiny capacitor, reached through one transistor. With no circuit to restore it, the charge leaks away, so every row is read and rewritten every 32 ms. Drawn generically: the card's DRAM is made on a DRAM process, not TSMC N7, and its generation is not known.

p.atom.name: A silicon atom
p.atom.blurb: One of the crystal's atoms: a tiny nucleus with 14 electrons around it. Only the outer four take part in bonds and in electronics; the other ten sit deep inside, held 20 to 300 times more tightly.

p.dopant.name: A dopant atom: phosphorus in the crystal
p.dopant.blurb: A foreign atom in a silicon atom's place. Phosphorus brings five outer electrons, one more than the bonds need, and that spare electron is free to carry current; boron brings three, leaving a gap (a hole) that carries current the other way. This is how a transistor's source and drain are made to conduct.

p.nucleus.name: The silicon-28 nucleus
p.nucleus.blurb: Fourteen protons and fourteen neutrons, packed together by the strong force: a thirty-thousandth of the atom's width but 99.97% of its mass. Nothing in a chip ever touches it.

p.nucleon.name: A proton
p.nucleon.blurb: A proton is three quarks (up, up, down) held by gluons; a neutron is up, down, down. Unlike the electron, it has a real size, because it is a bound state, and most of its mass is the energy of what goes on inside.

p.quark.name: A quark

bound.words: no size measured: a radius under 4.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ m

p.quark.blurb: As far as any experiment can tell, a quark is a point. The disc here is only the limit: if a quark has a size, it is smaller than this, under a two-thousandth of the proton. Quarks are never found alone; pull one out and the energy makes new quarks.

p.electron.name: An electron

bound.words: no size measured: a radius under 2 × 10⁻²⁰ m

p.electron.blurb: The particle that carries every current in the chip. Its charge and mass are known to 10 digits, but no experiment has found any size: as far as we know it is a point. The 'cloud' of the atom is where the electron is likely to be, not the electron itself.

p.planck.name: The Planck length
p.planck.blurb: The length built from gravity, quantum mechanics and the speed of light. Here, physicists expect space and time themselves to need a quantum description that nobody has yet; whether anything can be smaller is unknown. Between the quark's limit and here lie 16 powers of ten that no experiment has reached.

p.wrap.name: The ring of sizes
p.wrap.blurb: This is not further out in space. The ring is a picture of every size at once, the smallest joined to the largest; the links across it are physics, not distance. Looking far out is looking back in time, to an early universe that was a sea of quarks.

bernal.name: Bernal Heights
bernal.blurb: Bernal Heights, a hill neighbourhood of about 26,000 people in south-east San Francisco. The hill is red chert: quartz, silicon dioxide, from the shells of plankton that lived 100 to 200 million years ago. Refined, the same silicon is the die. Light crosses the neighbourhood in 7.3 µs, about 4,400 of the chip's clock ticks.

st29.name: 29th Street
st29.blurb: 29th Street, 1.3 km long, drops about 95 m from the hills of Noe Valley to the flats where the Mission meets Bernal Heights. Light runs its length in 4.3 µs, about 2,600 ticks of the chip's clock.

studio45.name: Studio 45
studio45.blurb: Studio 45, a co-working space and workshop for people who build hardware: the lab's rack is here. Light crosses the building in 123 ns, 74 ticks of the chip's clock.
studio45.note: the building at its address, about 37 m deep and 9 m wide (DataSF building footprints); where the rack stands in it is not recorded

lib.nor2.name: NOR gate
lib.nor2.blurb: Out is 1 only when both inputs are 0: two p-type transistors in series pull it up, two n-type side by side pull it down. With the NAND, any logic can be built from it.

lib.aoi21.name: AND-OR-INVERT gate
lib.aoi21.blurb: One stage of transistors that computes not (A·B + C): cheaper and faster than an AND, an OR and an inverter. A fast adder's carry cells are made of these.

lib.shifter.name: Shifter (stages of multiplexers)
lib.shifter.blurb: Moves a number left or right by any number of places in a few steps: each stage shifts by 1, 2, 4, ... places or not. The multiply-add uses one to line up the numbers it adds and another to normalise the result.

lib.lzd.name: A leading-zero counter
lib.lzd.blurb: Counts the zeros before the first 1 of a number, in a tree of small cells: it tells the normaliser how far to shift a sum so that its first digit is a 1.

lib.decoder.name: Decoder
lib.decoder.blurb: Turns an address into one raised line: 3 bits pick one of 8 rows, 7 bits one of 128. Every memory and register file has one for its rows.

lib.regfile.name: Register file
lib.regfile.blurb: A small, fast memory with several doors: rows of latches, a decoder that picks the row to write, and multiplexers that read one row out per port. Processors keep their registers in these.

lib.logic.name: Control logic: standard cells
lib.logic.blurb: What any block of control logic is made of when its own netlist is not published: flip-flops that hold its state and a few kinds of gate that compute the next state, all from a library of standard cells.

lib.counter.name: Counter
lib.counter.blurb: A register that adds one to itself on every clock (or every event): flip-flops and a chain of half adders. Barrier counters, credit counters and performance counters are all of this kind.

lib.cmpeq.name: Equality comparator
lib.cmpeq.blurb: Says whether two numbers are equal: an XNOR gate per bit, then a tree of gates that is 1 only if every bit agreed. A cache uses one per way to find its hit.

lib.fifo.name: Queue (first in, first out)
lib.fifo.blurb: Where requests wait their turn: a small register file, a counter that points where the next one is written, another where the next one is read, and a compare that says full or empty.

lib.pll.name: A phase-locked loop (PLL)
lib.pll.blurb: Makes a fast clock from a slow, steady one: it compares the two, and nudges an oscillator (a ring of inverters) until its output, divided down, matches the reference.

lib.ecc.name: Error correction (SECDED)
lib.ecc.blurb: Extra check bits stored with the data, each the parity of some of the bits: on a read they show whether a bit flipped, which one, so it can be put right, and whether two did.

lib.rom.name: A read-only memory (ROM)
lib.rom.blurb: A table fixed when the chip is made: a transistor where a bit is 0, none where it is 1. The vector unit's transcendental functions read their coefficients from small tables like this.

lib.diffamp.name: A differential amplifier
lib.diffamp.blurb: Two matched transistors that share one current: the higher input takes more of it. It amplifies the difference between two wires and ignores what they share, which is how a receiver hears a weak signal through noise.

lib.xbar.name: A crossbar switch
lib.xbar.blurb: Connects any input to any output for one cycle: a multiplexer per output picks the input its arbiter chose. In the chip it is 512 bits wide, so it is mostly wires.

lib.round.name: Rounding
lib.round.blurb: The exact product and sum are longer than a float can keep: three extra bits say whether the kept part rounds up by one at its last place, to the nearest value, a tie to the even one.

lib.wire.name: Copper wiring, in section
lib.wire.blurb: The chip's finest wires are copper, about 20 nm wide and 40 nm apart, wrapped in a thin cobalt liner so that copper atoms do not wander; cobalt contacts take them down to the transistors.

lib.buck.name: A buck converter (a switching regulator)
lib.buck.blurb: How 12 volts becomes half a volt without burning the rest as heat: two transistors connect an inductor to 12 V or to ground, hundreds of thousands of times a second, and the inductor and a capacitor smooth the pulses into a steady supply.

lib.powerfet.name: A power transistor, in section
lib.powerfet.blurb: A switch for tens of amps: thousands of small transistor cells side by side, each passing current straight down through the silicon from its source on top to the drain underneath.

lib.strap.name: A boot switch and its pin
lib.strap.blurb: A switch on the card holds one of the chip's pins at 0 or lets a resistor pull it to 1; when the chip comes out of reset it reads the pin and starts accordingly.

p.cu.name: A copper atom
p.cu.blurb: Copper: 29 electrons around a nucleus of 29 protons. In the metal each atom gives its one outer electron to a shared sea that flows when a voltage pushes it: that is the current in every wire of the chip.

et.process.statement: The ET-SoC-1 is made in TSMC 7 nm.
et.process.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.process.quote: "The Esperanto supercomputer on a chip has been fabricated in TSMC 7-nm technology and contains over 24 billion transistors." (p. 37)

et.process-n7.statement: WikiChip names the process as TSMC N7 (the first-generation 7 nm, not N7+ with EUV); Esperanto's papers say only "TSMC 7 nm".
et.process-n7.source: D. Schor, "A Look At The ET-SoC-1, Esperanto's Massively Multi-Core RISC-V Approach To AI", WikiChip Fuse, 16 May 2021 (public 10 Jul 2021); read via the Internet Archive capture of 10 Jul 2021 (the site refuses connections)
et.process-n7.note: Whether the silicon is N7 or the IP-compatible N7P (same design rules) is not published.
et.process-n7.quote: "Physically, the chip is fabricated on TSMC's N7 process technology."

et.transistors.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.transistors.note: WikiChip (May 2021, before Hot Chips) gave 23.8 billion: "packing 23.8 billion transistors".
et.transistors.quote: "The ET-SoC-1 chip is implemented in TSMC 7-nm technology using over 24 billion transistors." (p. 31); Hot Chips 33 slide 20: "24 billion transistors"

et.die-area.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.die-area.quote: "It has a die area of 570 mm2 and uses 89 mask layers." (p. 37); slide 20: "Die-area: 570 mm2"

et.masks.statement: 89 mask layers: 89 photolithography steps define the wafer, from fins up to the top metal.
et.masks.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)

et.package.statement: The package is 45 x 45 mm, with 2,494 balls to the board and over 30,000 bumps to the die.
et.package.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.package.quote: "Package: 45x45mm with 2494 balls to PCB, over 30,000 bumps to die" (slide 20)

et.sram-bytes.statement: Over 160 million bytes of on-die SRAM (caches and scratchpads).
et.sram-bytes.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.sram-bytes.note: The datasheet's 140 MB is the 35 shire caches alone (repository fact chip.sram-total). Adding the 1,088 minion L1s (4 KiB) and 136 neighbourhood I-caches (32 KiB) gives about 156 million bytes; the rest (Maxion L1s, tags, ECC, buffers) is not itemised anywhere (inference).
et.sram-bytes.quote: "Over 160 million bytes of on-die SRAM used for caches and scratchpad memory" (slide 20)

et.cores.statement: 1,088 ET-Minion cores, 4 ET-Maxion cores and 1 service processor: 1,093 RISC-V cores.
et.cores.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.cores.quote: "1088 energy-efficient ET-Minion 64-bit RISC-V in-order cores each with a vector/tensor unit" / "4 high-performance ET-Maxion 64-bit RISC-V out-of-order cores" (slide 2); "1 RISC-V service processor" (slide 20)

et.range.statement: Operating range: ET-Minions 300 MHz to 2 GHz (typical 500 MHz to 1.5 GHz expected); the cards here run 600-800 MHz.
et.range.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.range.quote: "OPERATING RANGE: 300 MHz TO 2 GHz" (slide 7); "Typical operation 500 MHz to 1.5 GHz expected" (slide 20)

et.power.statement: Typical power under 20 W, adjustable from 10 to 60+ W in software.
et.power.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.power.quote: "Power typically < 20 watts, can be adjusted for 10 to 60+ watts under SW control" (slide 20)

et.shire-supplies.statement: Each minion shire has its own low-voltage supply inputs, so its voltage can be trimmed against threshold-voltage variation and for DVFS.
et.shire-supplies.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.shire-supplies.quote: "Each Minion Shire has independent low voltage power supply inputs that can be finely adjusted to mitigate Vt variation effects and enable DVFS" (slide 20)

et.nominal-075.statement: 0.75 V is "the nominal voltage in 7 nm" (Esperanto); TSMC's N7 core transistors are designed around it.
et.nominal-075.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.nominal-075.quote: "Reducing the operating voltage to 0.75 V, the nominal voltage in 7 nm, would result in 164 W, still way too high." (p. 33)

et.sweet-spot.statement: Esperanto's chosen region: minions between 300 and 500 mV, near the best energy efficiency (0.3 V gave 20x the efficiency of the highest voltage in their model).
et.sweet-spot.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.sweet-spot.note: The voltage curve is modelled, with cores re-synthesised at each voltage (repository R6).
et.sweet-spot.quote: "Esperanto's sweet spot for achieving best performance will usually be for operating our ET-Minions between 300 and 500 mV, that is, nearest the best energy efficiency points." (p. 33)

et.lib-04.statement: The standard-cell libraries were re-characterised at 0.4 V for the timing tools; the pipeline has very few gates per stage to keep MHz up at low voltage.
et.lib-04.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.lib-04.quote: "The core uses an in-order pipeline optimized to have very few gates per pipeline stage to improve megahertz when operated at low voltages. For timing and other CAD tools, we had libraries recharacterized at 0.4 V." (p. 33)

et.one-plane.statement: The whole minion, its 4 KB L1 included, is on one low-voltage power plane.
et.one-plane.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.one-plane.quote: "To simplify physical design, the entire ET-Minion, including its 4-KB L1 caches, operates on a single low-voltage power plane." (p. 33)

et.custom-sram.statement: Esperanto designed its own low-voltage memory cells instead of TSMC's standard SRAM for the minion: larger cells that work far below nominal voltage, around 400 mV. (The repository finds the minion L1 and register files are latch arrays.)
et.custom-sram.source: D. Schor, "A Look At The ET-SoC-1, Esperanto's Massively Multi-Core RISC-V Approach To AI", WikiChip Fuse, 16 May 2021 (public 10 Jul 2021); read via the Internet Archive capture of 10 Jul 2021 (the site refuses connections)
et.custom-sram.note: Art Swift (Esperanto CEO) quoted by WikiChip. Repository: the L1 is an LRAM latch array (memory-levels fact l1:l1.lram-model and research-inside.md).
et.custom-sram.quote: "Esperanto has gone further and designed its own custom SRAM instead of using TSMC's standard SRAM offering. The cells, while physically larger, can stably operate at considerably lower voltage - far below nominal. 'When I talk about low voltage operations, I really mean operating at much lower than nominal voltages. So, if nominal is 0.75 V or so, we are operating on the order of 400 mV,' Swift said."

et.sram-nominal.statement: The shire's four 1 MB SRAM banks run near the process-nominal voltage, for density; the mesh has its own low-voltage domain.
et.sram-nominal.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.sram-nominal.quote: "These SRAM banks operate near the process-nominal supply voltage to allow higher density than the smaller caches within each core." / "Shires are connected to each other via an on-chip mesh interconnect operated on its own low-voltage domain." (p. 35)

et.wires-slow.statement: 7 nm wires are slow, so minions were grouped in eights (neighbourhoods) before wire length became a problem.
et.wires-slow.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.wires-slow.quote: "Physical design plays an important role in chip architecture as 7-nm wires are relatively slow. We found it convenient to group eight ET-Minion cores together before wire length became a problem." (p. 34)

et.cdyn-target.statement: Esperanto's target: 10 mW per minion at 1 GHz and 0.425 V, i.e. 0.04 nF switched per cycle (vs 2.2 nF for a 3 GHz x86 core).
et.cdyn-target.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.cdyn-target.quote: "10mW ET-Minion core (~10W for 1K cores) 0.01 W 1 GHz 0.425v 0.04nF" (slide 5); "Power (Watts) = Cdynamic x Voltage2 x Frequency + Leakage"

et.ops-per-ghz.statement: Each minion peaks at 128 int8 operations per cycle (128 GOPS per GHz); 16 fp32 or 32 fp16 operations per cycle.
et.ops-per-ghz.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021
et.ops-per-ghz.quote: "Each ET-Minion can deliver peak of 128 Int8 GOPS per GHz"; "16 32-bit single precision operations per cycle"; "32 16-bit half precision operations per cycle" (slide 7)

et.tensor-512.statement: A tensor instruction runs for up to 512 cycles while the integer pipeline sleeps.
et.tensor-512.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.tensor-512.quote: "Esperanto added new tensor instructions that utilize the full vector width every cycle and run for up to 512 cycles." / "During these long tensor instructions, the RISC-V integer pipeline is put to sleep" (pp. 33-34)

et.trans-rom.statement: The transcendental unit is ROM-based, trading area for low power.
et.trans-rom.source: D. Schor, "A Look At The ET-SoC-1, Esperanto's Massively Multi-Core RISC-V Approach To AI", WikiChip Fuse, 16 May 2021 (public 10 Jul 2021); read via the Internet Archive capture of 10 Jul 2021 (the site refuses connections)
et.trans-rom.quote: "The trans unit is ROM-based, favoring lower power over silicon."

et.vt-area.statement: In Esperanto's minion plot (drawn roughly to scale) the vector/tensor unit takes far more area than the integer pipeline.
et.vt-area.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), same title, IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022, pp. 31-38 (hosted by Esperanto)
et.vt-area.quote: "you can see that the vector/tensor unit takes far more area than the integer pipeline" (p. 33, Figure 2)

et.icache.statement: Eight minions share one 32 KB instruction cache.
et.icache.source: D. Ditzel et al. (Esperanto), "Accelerating ML Recommendation with over a Thousand RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", Hot Chips 33 slides, 24 Aug 2021

et.density.statement: Average density 24 billion / 570 mm² = 42 million transistors per mm², 46% of N7's densest logic (91.2 MTr/mm²): SRAM periphery, analog (PLLs, PHYs), I/O and wiring take the rest.
et.density.source: arithmetic on et.transistors, et.die-area and n7.density-hd

et.tr-per-minion.statement: At most about 15 million transistors per minion: what is left after the shire caches' bitcells (35 x 4 MiB x 6 transistors = 7.0 billion), shared over 1,088 minions; the true count is lower because the rest also holds the mesh, memory shires, PHYs, PCIe and Maxions.
et.tr-per-minion.note: Assumes 6-transistor cells for the shire caches (the bitcell is not documented: memory-levels u.bitcell). No floorplan below the shire is published.

et.v-minion.statement: Minion rail: 0.517 V at 600 MHz on die (0.568 V at 700, 0.618 V at 800); firmware limits 0.40-0.62 V.
et.v-minion.quote: "Three operating points: 600 MHz at 0.517 V, 700 at 0.568, 800 at 0.618." (16-dvfs-and-leakage.md)

et.v-sram.statement: SRAM rail (shire-cache arrays): 0.703-0.707 V on die; firmware limits 0.66-0.85 V.
et.v-sram.source: repository: chip facts volt.sram; memory-levels l2:l2.voltage.idle, l2:l2.voltage.limits

et.v-noc.statement: Mesh rail: 0.485 V set point, 0.483-0.486 V on die.

et.v-other.statement: Other rails on die: DDR (memory shires) 0.76-0.77 V, Maxion 0.58-0.59 V, I/O shire 0.75 V, PCIe shire 0.75 V; LPDDR4X VDDQ 1.1 V, VDDQLP 0.64 V.

et.per-shire-v.statement: Per-shire minion-rail voltage at idle: 513-522 mV across the 34 minion shires.

et.leakage.statement: Leakage on aifoundry2 at 80 °C: 20-29 W, 55-80% of an idle card and 31-45% of a 64 W random-data matmul; it rises 0.65 W per °C (fit: 23.3 W x exp((T-80)/36)).
et.leakage.source: repository: docs/findings/16-dvfs-and-leakage.md (Kanter table row "Leakage is typically 5-30%"); docs/research/why-low-power.md "What this card measures"
et.leakage.quote: "Fitted: 12.6 W fixed + 23.3 W x exp((T - 80)/36) of leakage" (why-low-power.md)

et.leak-double.statement: By that fit, leakage doubles every 25 °C.

et.leak-per-tr.statement: Spread over 24 billion transistors, 23 W of leakage is about 1 nW each: roughly 1.4-1.9 nA, about 10 billion electrons a second through every transistor that is "off".
et.leak-per-tr.note: An average over every kind of transistor and rail: SRAM, logic, analog; the leakage is not split by rail.

et.cdyn-measured.statement: Measured switched capacitance per minion: 0.168 nF on random fp32 matmul (0.064 on ones, 0.012 on zeros), against the 0.04 nF target.
et.cdyn-measured.quote: "Cdynamic = P/(V^2 f): 0.012, 0.064 and 0.168 nF against the slide's 0.04 nF target"

et.electrons-per-cycle.statement: Each cycle of a minion on random fp32 matmul moves about 87 pC from the 0.517 V supply: 540 million electrons per minion per cycle (45 pJ).

et.flip-reg.statement: Clocking one register bit in the tensor unit costs 3.18 fJ (fitted on aifoundry2): at 0.517 V that is an effective 11.9 fF charged, about 38,000 electrons from the supply.
et.flip-reg.source: repository: docs/energy-manual/03-instructions.md "Where the tensor unit's energy goes: per flip" (ffclk 3.179 fJ)
et.flip-reg.note: Treats each clocking event as one full charge from the supply (E = C V^2); the effective capacitance includes the clock wiring and buffers that drive the flip-flop, not only the flip-flop.

n7.start.statement: TSMC started N7 volume production in April 2018; first products include the Apple A12, Kirin 980, Snapdragon 855 and AMD Zen 2.
n7.start.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.start.quote: "TSMC started mass production of their 7-nanometer node in April 2018. Since then we have seen a number of high-profile processors that make use of the technology including the Apple A12 and A12X, the Kirin 980, and soon Qualcomm's Snapdragon 855 and AMD Zen 2."

n7.generation.statement: N7 is TSMC's 4th-generation FinFET and 5th-generation high-k metal gate: gate-last, with two gate-oxide thicknesses (thin for core logic, thick for I/O).
n7.generation.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.generation.note: What the two oxides are used for (core vs I/O transistors) is the usual meaning of "dual gate oxide"; TSMC does not say (generic).
n7.generation.quote: "This is a fourth-generation FinFET, fifth-generation HKMG, gate-last, dual gate oxide process."

n7.litho.statement: N7 is patterned with 193 nm immersion (DUV) light, no EUV: fins by self-aligned quadruple patterning, gates and M0-M4 by double patterning.
n7.litho.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.litho.quote: "For the 7-nanometer process, deep ultraviolet (DUV) 193 nm ArF Immersion lithography continues to be used." Design rules: Fin 30 SAQP; Poly 57 SADP; M0-M4 40 SADP; M5-M9 76 Single.

n7.vs-n16.statement: TSMC: N7 gives about 30% more speed, 55% less power or 3x the logic density of its 16 nm.
n7.vs-n16.note: The IEDM 2016 paper said 35-40% speed or >65% power and >3.3x routed gate density (ew-iedm16, dj-iedm16).
n7.vs-n16.quote: "delivers up to a 30% speed improvement, a 55% power saving, and a 3 times logic density improvement over 16nm (N16) technology"

n7.fin-pitch.statement: Fin pitch 30 nm (fins patterned by self-aligned quadruple patterning).
n7.fin-pitch.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.fin-pitch.note: Also Wikipedia, "7 nm process" (TSMC N7 fin pitch 30 nm).
n7.fin-pitch.quote: Transistor Profile table: "Fin Pitch | 36 nm | 30 nm | 0.83x" (10 nm, 7 nm); design rules "Fin | 30 | SAQP"

n7.fin-width.statement: Fin width 6 nm (the same as TSMC 10 nm).
n7.fin-width.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.fin-width.note: Fins are tapered, wider at the base, with rounded tops (Siliconics on Intel 14 nm: "Vertical fins! But still rounded fin tops"; Intel 10 nm: "fin width 5-15 nm, ~7 nm at half height"); WikiChip does not say at what height its 6 nm is measured.
n7.fin-width.quote: Transistor Profile table: "Fin Width | 6 nm | 6 nm | 1.00x"

n7.fin-height.statement: Fin height 52 nm (42 nm at TSMC 10 nm): taller fins carry more current per footprint.
n7.fin-height.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.fin-height.note: The height of fin standing above the isolation oxide, as these tables quote it (not stated explicitly).
n7.fin-height.quote: Transistor Profile table: "Fin Height | 42 nm | 52 nm | 1.24x"; "Continuing to scale the fin width gives you a narrower channel while increasing the height to maintain a good effective width is done in order to improve the short channel characteristics and subthreshold slope"

n7.weff.statement: One fin gives about 110 nm of channel width: the gate wraps both 52 nm sides and the 6 nm top. N7 has over twice N16's effective width.
n7.weff.source: C. Hu, ch. 7 (the rule) with n7.fin-height and n7.fin-width
n7.weff.quote: Hu: "The channel width, W, is the sum of twice the fin height and the width of the fin." 2 x 52 + 6 = 110 nm. WikiChip: "Compared to N16, N7 has over twice the effective channel width."

n7.cpp.statement: Contacted gate pitch 57 nm in the dense cells (64 nm in the 7.5-track high-performance cells).
n7.cpp.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.cpp.note: WikiChip: "while at IEDM TSMC reported slightly more aggressive pitches, the numbers shown in this article are the actual pitches used in their standard cells"; Dick James speculated 54 nm from the IEDM paper.
n7.cpp.quote: "For the transistor, the gate pitch has been further scaled down to 57 nm, however, the interconnect pitch halted at the 40 nm point in order to keep patterning at the SADP point." Flavors table: Gate Pitch 57 nm (low power) / 64 nm (high performance)

n7.leff.statement: Effective gate length about 16.5 nm: the length of channel the gate controls, between source and drain.
n7.leff.source: D. James (TechInsights/Chipworks), "IEDM 2016 - Setting the Stage for 7.5 nm", Solid State Technology "Real Chips" blog, 18 Jan 2017 (on S.-Y. Wu et al. (TSMC), "A 7nm CMOS platform technology featuring 4th generation FinFET transistors with a 0.027um2 high density 6-T SRAM cell for mobile SoC applications", IEDM 2016, paper 2.6)
n7.leff.note: The physical (drawn) gate length is not published; comparable: TSMC 10 nm minimum Lg ~25 nm, Intel 10 nm 18 nm (Siliconics).
n7.leff.quote: "fifth-generation HKMG gate-last, dual gate oxide process ... effective gate length (leff) centered around 16.5 nm"

n7.ss.statement: Subthreshold swing about 65 mV per decade: below threshold, each 65 mV less on the gate cuts the current tenfold (the room-temperature limit is 60).
n7.ss.source: D. James (TechInsights/Chipworks), "IEDM 2016 - Setting the Stage for 7.5 nm", Solid State Technology "Real Chips" blog, 18 Jan 2017 (on S.-Y. Wu et al. (TSMC), "A 7nm CMOS platform technology featuring 4th generation FinFET transistors with a 0.027um2 high density 6-T SRAM cell for mobile SoC applications", IEDM 2016, paper 2.6)
n7.ss.quote: "Sub-threshold swing has been pushed down to ~65mV/decade, and DIBL is ~40 mV/V"

n7.dibl.statement: Drain-induced barrier lowering about 40 mV/V: raising the drain voltage by 1 V lowers the threshold by about 40 mV.
n7.dibl.source: D. James (TechInsights/Chipworks), "IEDM 2016 - Setting the Stage for 7.5 nm", Solid State Technology "Real Chips" blog, 18 Jan 2017 (on S.-Y. Wu et al. (TSMC), "A 7nm CMOS platform technology featuring 4th generation FinFET transistors with a 0.027um2 high density 6-T SRAM cell for mobile SoC applications", IEDM 2016, paper 2.6)

n7.vt-options.statement: Four threshold-voltage options spanning about 200 mV, set by different gate metals (faster but leakier, or slower and tighter).
n7.vt-options.source: D. James (TechInsights/Chipworks), "IEDM 2016 - Setting the Stage for 7.5 nm", Solid State Technology "Real Chips" blog, 18 Jan 2017 (on S.-Y. Wu et al. (TSMC), "A 7nm CMOS platform technology featuring 4th generation FinFET transistors with a 0.027um2 high density 6-T SRAM cell for mobile SoC applications", IEDM 2016, paper 2.6)
n7.vt-options.note: The absolute threshold voltages are not published (unknown); which options the ET-SoC-1 uses is not published either.
n7.vt-options.quote: "four device Vt options with a range of ~200 mV"; WikiChip: "Different multi-Vt devices were developed for this process with a Vt range of around 200 mV."

n7.vt-abs.statement: N7's absolute threshold voltages are not published. Running at 0.4-0.52 V and libraries characterised at 0.4 V imply the minion's transistors switch with a few hundred millivolts or less of threshold: near-threshold operation.
n7.vt-abs.source: open question; the inputs are et.lib-04, et.sweet-spot, et.v-minion

n7.mmp.statement: Metal pitch 40 nm for M0 to M4 (so the finest wires are about 20 nm wide), 76 nm for M5 to M9, 124 nm for M10, 720 nm for M11-M12.
n7.mmp.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.mmp.note: The IEDM paper as Dick James read it: "1x metal pitch is 40 nm for M0 to M4, and M5 - M9 are 1.9x (76 nm)". Line width ~half the pitch is the usual layout (generic).
n7.mmp.quote: Design rules: "M0 | 40 | SADP", "M1-M4 | 40 | SADP | 1x", "M5-M9 | 76 | Single | 1.9x", "M10 | 124 | Single | 3.1x", "M11, M12 | 720 | Single | 18x"

n7.metal-layers.statement: The interconnect is a stack of about a dozen copper layers in low-k insulator: TSMC's paper says 12 layers; WikiChip's design rules list M0-M12. How many the ET-SoC-1 uses is not published.
n7.metal-layers.source: D. James (TechInsights/Chipworks), "IEDM 2016 - Setting the Stage for 7.5 nm", Solid State Technology "Real Chips" blog, 18 Jan 2017 (on S.-Y. Wu et al. (TSMC), "A 7nm CMOS platform technology featuring 4th generation FinFET transistors with a 0.027um2 high density 6-T SRAM cell for mobile SoC applications", IEDM 2016, paper 2.6)
n7.metal-layers.quote: "193 nm immersion lithography, dual raised source/drain epi, a novel contact technique, and a 12-layer copper/low-k interconnect stack"

n7.contacts-co.statement: Contacts to source and drain are cobalt: TSMC replaced tungsten with cobalt fill in the trench contacts, halving their resistance.
n7.contacts-co.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.contacts-co.note: WikiChip shows MSS Corp's element map of the Apple A12 (N7) with cobalt contacts.
n7.contacts-co.quote: "Like Intel, TSMC introduced cobalt fill at the trench contact, replacing the tungsten contact. This has the effect of reducing the resistance at that area by 50%."; Dick James (2022): "both TSMC and Samsung have cobalt contacts in their 7- and 5-nm products."

n7.cu-co-liner.statement: The finest copper wires have a cobalt liner and cap (TSMC since 16FF's M1-M3, every generation since, including N5): the cobalt keeps copper atoms from migrating.
n7.cu-co-liner.source: P. Singer with D. James (TechInsights), "Intel 4 Process Drops Cobalt Interconnect, Goes with Tried and Tested Copper with Cobalt Liner/Cap", Semiconductor Digest, 1 Oct 2022
n7.cu-co-liner.note: "keeps copper atoms from migrating" paraphrases the electromigration benefit the article attributes to cobalt (Intel: "improved electromigration (EM) 5 - 10x").
n7.cu-co-liner.quote: "When we looked at the Apple A9 the following year, in TSMC's 16FF process, the M1 - M3 layers had Co liners and caps" / "And in fact, it has been used in the minimum pitch metals every generation since then, including the N5"

n7.cells.statement: Standard cells are 240 nm tall (high density, 6 tracks, 8 fin pitches, 57 nm gate pitch) or 300 nm (high performance, 7.5 tracks, 10 fin pitches, 64 nm gate pitch); a 360 nm 9-track variant also exists.
n7.cells.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.cells.note: Which library the ET-SoC-1 uses is not published; the RTL names cell families HDBULT08 and HDBULT11 (memory-levels fact l1:l1.icg-cells, an open question l1:l1.u-library).
n7.cells.quote: "TSMC 7-nanometer comes in two variations - low power and high performance. Those cells are 240 nm and 300 nm tall respectively." Flavors: "240 nm 8-fin x 30 nm" / "300 nm 10-fin x 30 nm"; Tracks 6 T / 7.5 T

n7.two-fin.statement: In the 240 nm dense cell each transistor typically has 2 fins (Angstronomics' "2-fin" N7 cell).
n7.two-fin.note: 8 fin pitches per cell: about 2 active fins for the PMOS row and 2 for the NMOS row, the rest under the power rails and the gap (generic layout).
n7.two-fin.quote: N7 2-fin descriptor "H240g57" (H240 = 240nm cell height, g57 = 57nm contacted gate pitch)

n7.density-hd.statement: Densest logic: about 91.2 million transistors per mm² (high-performance cells about 65).
n7.density-hd.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.density-hd.quote: "The dense cells come at around 91.2 MTr/mm² while the less dense, high-performance cells, are calculated at around 65 MTr/mm²."

n7.sram-hd.statement: High-density 6-transistor SRAM bitcell: 0.027 µm² (TSMC's IEDM 2016 headline).
n7.sram-hd.source: D. Schor, "TSMC 7nm HD and HP Cells, 2nd Gen 7nm, And The Snapdragon 855 DTCO", WikiChip Fuse, 16 Jun 2019 (VLSI 2019); read via the Internet Archive capture of 13 Nov 2019
n7.sram-hd.note: WikiChip's 7 nm table leaves TSMC's high-performance (high-current) cell blank: not published.
n7.sram-hd.quote: "Here, the 7-nanometer high-density SRAM bitcell is 0.027 µm², making it the second-densest cell reported to date. On the current FinFET processes, the bitcells are largely fin-quantized."

n7.sram-dims.statement: A 0.027 µm² cell fits 2 gate pitches by 8 fin pitches: about 114 x 240 nm, one fin per transistor in the densest cell.
n7.sram-dims.note: A layout reading, not a published drawing. The one-fin-per-transistor (1:1:1) arrangement is the usual high-density cell (generic). Which bitcell the ET-SoC-1's macros use is not documented (memory-levels u.bitcell).

n7.sram-vmin.statement: TSMC's 256 Mbit N7 SRAM test chip read and wrote down to 0.5 V.
n7.sram-vmin.source: D. Manners, "7nm processes at IEDM", Electronics Weekly, 20 Oct 2016 (republished by Design & Reuse), on the TSMC IEDM 2016 paper 2.6
n7.sram-vmin.note: The ET-SoC-1 runs its shire-cache arrays at 0.705 V (et.v-sram).
n7.sram-vmin.quote: "a fully functional, low-voltage 256Mb SRAM test chip with full read/write functionality down to 0.5V, and the smallest SRAM cells ever reported (0.027um2)"

n7.features.statement: TSMC's list of what makes N7: an optimised fin width and profile, raised source/drain epitaxy that strains the channel, a novel contact process, and copper/low-k wiring.
n7.features.source: D. Manners, "7nm processes at IEDM", Electronics Weekly, 20 Oct 2016 (republished by Design & Reuse), on the TSMC IEDM 2016 paper 2.6
n7.features.quote: "an advanced patterning technique used with 193nm immersion lithography, an optimized fin width and profile, a raised source/drain epitaxial process that strains the transistor channel and reduces parasitics, a novel contact process, and a copper/low-k interconnect scheme featuring different metal pitches and stacks."

n7.hpc.statement: TSMC's symposium: N7 gives +33% performance at the same leakage as N16FFC, or 58% less leakage at the same drive.
n7.hpc.source: T. Dillinger, "Top 10 Updates from the TSMC Technology Symposium, Part II", SemiWiki, 23 Mar 2017
n7.hpc.quote: "N7 will provide a +33% performance boost at the same I_off compared to N16FFC, or a -58% I_off leakage reduction at the same I_on."

cmp.gf7.statement: GlobalFoundries' 7 nm (IEDM 2017): fin pitch 30 nm, gate pitch 56 nm, metal pitch 40 nm, four work-function metals for each of N and P; active fin about 41 nm tall and 6 nm wide; cobalt contacts; up to 17 metal layers.
cmp.gf7.source: D. James (Siliconics), "A Quick Look at 14-nm and 10-nm", AVS Joint Users Group, July 2018 (JTG718-4)
cmp.gf7.quote: "IEDM 2017 paper states FP 30 nm, CGP 56 nm, MMP 40 nm, quad-WF NFETs & PFETs"; "Active fin height ~41 nm, width ~6 nm, gate width ~ 88 nm"; "Co contacts, up to 17 metal layers" (slide 25)

cmp.intel10.statement: Intel 10 nm: fin height 46-53 nm, fin width 5-15 nm from top to bottom (about 7 nm at half height); punch-through stopper by solid-source diffusion; 4-6 work-function metals; cobalt M0 and M1.
cmp.intel10.source: D. James (Siliconics), "A Quick Look at 14-nm and 10-nm", AVS Joint Users Group, July 2018 (JTG718-4)
cmp.intel10.quote: "Fin height up from 34 to 42 to 53 nm, (IEDM17 46 nm) fin width 5 - 15 nm, ~7 nm at half height." / "Solid-source diffusion punch-stopper used again" / "Gate stack looks similar, 5th generation HKMG but 4 - 6 WFs" / "Cobalt M0 & M1 (with Ru?), Co cap on M2 - M5" (slides 12-13)

cmp.tsmc10.statement: TSMC 10 nm (Apple A11): fin pitch about 33 nm, fin width about 6 nm, gate height about 44 nm; fins visibly tapered.
cmp.tsmc10.source: D. James (Siliconics), "A Quick Look at 14-nm and 10-nm", AVS Joint Users Group, July 2018 (JTG718-4)
cmp.tsmc10.quote: "SAQP minimum fin pitch ~33 nm, fin width ~6 nm, functional gate height ~44 nm, gate width ~95 nm" (slide 18); "Fin taper" (slide 17 label)

gate.hfo2.statement: The gate insulator is hafnium oxide (HfO2, relative permittivity ~24, six times SiO2's 3.9) on a thin SiO2 interfacial layer: as good as 1 nm of SiO2 electrically, but thick enough that electrons cannot tunnel through.
gate.hfo2.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 7 (author's free chapter)
gate.hfo2.note: TSMC does not publish N7's stack or its thicknesses.
gate.hfo2.quote: "HfO2 has a relative dielectric constant (k) of ~24, six times larger than that of SiO2. A 6 nm thick HfO2 film is equivalent to 1 nm thick SiO2 ... These problems are minimized by inserting a thin SiO2 interfacial layer between the silicon substrate and the high-k dielectric."

gate.eot.statement: Equivalent oxide thickness under 1 nm is typical of FinFETs of this generation (0.7 nm in a 15 nm-gate research FinFET); N7's is not published.
gate.eot.source: X. Zhang, "Simulation-based Study of Super-steep Retrograde Doped Bulk FinFET Technology and 6T-SRAM Yield", UC Berkeley EECS Technical Report UCB/EECS-2016-3, 5 Jan 2016
gate.eot.note: A simulation study's parameters, not a TSMC figure.

gate.metals.statement: Gate metals: since the first high-k gates (45 nm), the n-type gate uses TiAl and the p-type TiN on HfO2, deposited into the trench left by a removed dummy polysilicon gate and filled with W or Al; their work functions (about 4.1 and 4.85 eV) set the threshold.
gate.metals.source: C. Zhao and J. Xiang, "Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) of Metal Gates for CMOS", Applied Sciences 9 (2019) 2388
gate.metals.note: Industry practice, not a TSMC N7 disclosure; multi-Vt options come from different work-function metal stacks (four per polarity in GF 7 nm, cmp.gf7).
gate.metals.quote: "In the 45 nm node, the first generation of the high-k/metal gate technology for mass production, dual metal/single high-k stack was used. The metal gate for nMOS was TiAl, and that for pMOS was TiN, integrated with HfO2 dielectric by a gate last process ... To fill the gap, a conductive metal such as Al or W was deposited." / "The PVD TiAl and PVD TiN in gate stacks with HfO2 show EWF around 4.1 eV and 4.85 eV."

gate.undoped-vt.statement: In a FinFET with an undoped channel the threshold voltage is set mainly by the gate metal's work function, not by dopants in the channel.
gate.undoped-vt.source: C. Zhao and J. Xiang, "Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) of Metal Gates for CMOS", Applied Sciences 9 (2019) 2388
gate.undoped-vt.quote: "The relation between Vt and the work function of the gate electrode for FinFETs with undoped channel is different to that for the planar MOSFETs. For planar devices, there are plenty of charges to form inversion. For undoped FinFETs, much less charges are available."

gate.cap-fin.statement: One fin's gate is a capacitor of roughly 60-90 aF (0.06-0.09 fF): 110 nm of wrapped width by 16.5 nm of length at an equivalent oxide of 0.7-1 nm.
gate.cap-fin.source: arithmetic on n7.weff, n7.leff and gate.eot
gate.cap-fin.note: Oxide capacitance only; the real gate also has overlap and fringe capacitance to the contacts (adds), and quantum effects that thin the inversion charge (subtracts).
gate.cap-fin.quote: C = 3.9 x 8.854e-12 F/m / EOT x (110 nm x 16.5 nm) = 63 aF at 1 nm, 90 aF at 0.7 nm

dope.channel.statement: The channel inside the fin is left undoped or lightly doped: the gate surrounds it on three sides, so there is no need for heavy doping.
dope.channel.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 7 (author's free chapter)
dope.channel.quote: "There is no need for heavy doping in the channel to reduce Wdep. This leads to low vertical field and less impurity scattering; as a result the mobility is higher"

dope.levels.statement: Fin doping in bulk FinFETs: about 1e18 cm^-3 with a conventional implant, about 1e16 with a super-steep retrograde profile; a punch-through stopper of 2.5-5e18 at the base of the fin blocks leakage under the channel.
dope.levels.source: X. Zhang, "Simulation-based Study of Super-steep Retrograde Doped Bulk FinFET Technology and 6T-SRAM Yield", UC Berkeley EECS Technical Report UCB/EECS-2016-3, 5 Jan 2016
dope.levels.note: TCAD study values; TSMC's profile is not published. Intel 10 nm uses a solid-source diffusion punch-stopper (cmp.intel10).
dope.levels.quote: "If a bulk-silicon wafer is used as the substrate, heavy doping is needed at the base of the fins to suppress off-state leakage current (Ioff). However, a conventional doping process results in dopants within the fin (channel region), on the order of 1 x 10^18 cm^-3." Table 1.1: Nfin 1e18 (control) / 1e16 (SSR); Nfin,peak 2.5e18 / 5e18; NSD 2e20

dope.n-sd.statement: NMOS source and drain: phosphorus-doped silicon grown epitaxially, up to 1.75e21 P atoms per cm³ (about 3% of the atoms), of which only about 1.3e20 are electrically active.
dope.n-sd.source: X. Li, A. Dube, Z. Ye, S. Sharma, Y. Kim, S. Chu (Applied Materials), "Selective Epitaxial Si:P Film for nMOSFET Application: High Phosphorous Concentration and High Tensile Strain", ECS/SMEQ joint meeting, Cancun, Oct 2014 (abstract)
dope.n-sd.note: Applied Materials' research film (2014), representative of FinFET Si:P source/drain epitaxy; TSMC's values are not published.
dope.n-sd.quote: "total [P] by SIMS in HS Si:P epitaxial film is 1.75E+21 at/cc (~ 3 at.% in silicon)"; "only ~1.3E+20 at/cc phosphorous atoms are electrically active"

dope.p-sd.statement: PMOS source and drain: boron-doped silicon-germanium, with boron above 1e20 per cm³ (patent ranges run to about 2e20 and beyond); the larger germanium atoms squeeze the channel, which speeds holes.
dope.p-sd.source: Qualcomm, US patent 9,564,518 B2, "Method and apparatus for source-drain junction formation in a FinFET with in-situ doping" (priority 24 Sep 2014)
dope.p-sd.note: A patent range, not a product measurement. The strain statement is generic: TSMC calls its epitaxy one "that strains the transistor channel" (n7.features).
dope.p-sd.quote: "one example range of boron concentration that may be used in forming a SiGeB epi layer ... may span from, for example, less than 1E20 at/cm3 and may encompass, for example, greater than 2E20 at/cm3."

dope.donor-acceptor.statement: Dopants work by valence: phosphorus or arsenic (5 outer electrons) gives one free electron (a donor); boron (3) leaves a hole (an acceptor). Freeing the extra electron takes only about 50 meV, about twice kT at room temperature, so dopants are almost all ionised.
dope.donor-acceptor.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 1 (author's free chapter)
dope.donor-acceptor.quote: "group V elements such as As ... bring five valence electrons with each atom. While four electrons are shared with the neighboring Si atoms, the fifth electron may escape to become a mobile electron, leaving behind a positive As ion." / "it takes the donor ionization energy (about 50 meV) to free the extra electron"

dope.count-channel.statement: A channel 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm holds about 257,000 silicon atoms but only 0.05 to 5 dopant atoms (at 1e16 to 1e18 per cm³): often none. That is why random dopant fluctuation would wreck such a device if it relied on channel doping.
dope.count-channel.source: arithmetic on n7.fin-width, n7.leff, n7.fin-height, si.density and dope.levels
dope.count-channel.note: Uses Leff for the length; the drawn gate is a little longer.

dope.count-sd.statement: At 1.75e21 per cm³ the source and drain hold 1.75 phosphorus atoms per cubic nanometre, one atom in 30.
dope.count-sd.quote: 1.75e21 cm^-3 x 1e-21 cm³/nm³ = 1.75 /nm³; / 49.9 Si per nm³ = 3.5%

si.lattice.statement: Silicon is a diamond-cubic crystal with a 0.5431 nm cube; every atom bonds to four neighbours 0.235 nm away.
si.lattice.source: NIST, CODATA 2022 recommended values, "lattice parameter of silicon"
si.lattice.note: Bond length a x sqrt(3)/4 = 0.2352 nm (derived).
si.lattice.quote: "5.431 020 511(89) x 10^-10 m" (CODATA 2022); Hu ch. 1: "each and every silicon atom has four other silicon atoms as its nearest neighbor atoms"

si.density.statement: 5 x 10^22 silicon atoms per cm³: 50 per cubic nanometre.
si.density.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Basic parameters of Silicon (Si)" (read via the mirror at www-f9.ijs.si)
si.density.quote: "Number of atoms in 1 cm3: 5*10^22"; "Lattice constant: 5.431 A"; "Dielectric constant: 11.7"; "Crystal structure: Diamond"

si.planes-width.statement: Across a 6 nm fin there are about 31 planes of atoms (11 unit cells); along a 16.5 nm channel about 86 planes (30 unit cells); up a 52 nm fin about 383 planes (96 unit cells).
si.planes-width.source: arithmetic on si.lattice, n7.fin-width, n7.leff, n7.fin-height
si.planes-width.note: Assumes the usual orientation: a (100) wafer, the channel along <110>, so fin sidewalls are (110) planes (an assumption; TSMC does not say).

si.bandgap.statement: Silicon's band gap is 1.12 eV at room temperature (1.11 eV at the card's 80 °C): an electron needs that much energy to leave a bond and conduct.
si.bandgap.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Band structure and carrier concentration of Silicon (Si)" (read via the mirror at www-f9.ijs.si; ioffe.ru served a self-signed certificate)
si.bandgap.note: At 353 K the formula gives 1.110 eV (derived).
si.bandgap.quote: "Energy gap 1.12 eV"; "Eg = 1.17 - 4.73*10^-4*T^2/(T+636) (eV)"; Hu ch. 1: "This band gap is 1.12 eV for Si."

si.ni.statement: Pure silicon has only about 1e10 free electrons per cm³ at room temperature (about 4e11 at 80 °C): in one 5,148 nm³ channel that is 0.00000005 electrons. Every carrier that conducts comes from the gate's field and the doped source and drain.
si.ni.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Band structure and carrier concentration of Silicon (Si)" (read via the mirror at www-f9.ijs.si; ioffe.ru served a self-signed certificate)
si.ni.note: At 80 °C: ni x (T/300)^1.5 x exp(-Eg/2kT ratio) = about 42x, 4e11 cm^-3 (derived); the count in a channel: 1e10 x 5.15e-18 = 5e-8.
si.ni.quote: "Intrinsic carrier concentration 1*10^10 cm-3"; Hu: "ni at room temperature is roughly 10^10 cm^-3 for Si"

si.mobility.statement: In pure silicon electrons move about 3 times more easily than holes (mobility up to 1,400 vs 450 cm²/V·s); electrons saturate at about 8e6 cm/s, so crossing a 16.5 nm channel takes about 0.2 ps.
si.mobility.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Electrical properties of Silicon (Si)" (read via the mirror at www-f9.ijs.si)
si.mobility.note: Transit time 16.5e-7 cm / 8e6 cm/s = 0.21 ps (derived), against a 1.67 ns cycle at 600 MHz.
si.mobility.quote: "Mobility electrons <=1400 cm2 V-1s-1"; "Mobility holes <=450 cm2 V-1s-1"; Hu ch. 6: "It is known that vsat is 8 x 10^6 cm/s for electrons and 6 x 10^6 cm/s for holes."

si.atom.statement: A silicon atom: 14 protons and 14 electrons, 4 of them valence electrons shared in bonds; 92.2% of silicon is silicon-28 (14 neutrons), 4.7% Si-29, 3.1% Si-30.
si.atom.source: NIST, "Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for Silicon"
si.atom.quote: "28Si 0.922 23(19)", "29Si 0.046 85(8)", "30Si 0.030 92(11)"; Hu ch. 1: "Silicon is a group IV element in the periodic table and has four valence electrons."

si.nucleus.statement: The silicon-28 nucleus has a charge radius of 3.12 fm (3.12 x 10^-15 m): about 75,000 times smaller than the 0.235 nm bond.
si.nucleus.source: K. Koenig et al., "Nuclear charge radii of silicon isotopes", arXiv:2309.02037, Table 1 (28Si from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99 (2013) 69-95)
si.nucleus.quote: 28Si charge radius "3.1224 (24)" fm (Table 1, from Angeli and Marinova 2013)

el.switch.statement: A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch: the gate voltage decides whether current flows between source and drain. Above threshold the gate's field pulls a thin layer of electrons (the inversion layer) to the fin's surfaces, connecting source to drain.
el.switch.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 6 (author's free chapter)
el.switch.quote: "At the most basic level, a MOSFET may be thought of as an on-off switch ... The gate voltage determines whether a current flows between the drain and source or not." / "When Vg is equal to Vdd ... an inversion layer is present"

el.off-not-off.statement: "Off" is not totally off: below the threshold the current falls only tenfold per 60 mV x eta (65 mV in N7). This subthreshold current is the leakage.
el.off-not-off.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 7 (author's free chapter)
el.off-not-off.quote: "At room temperature, the function exp(qVgs/kT) changes by 10 for every 60 mV change in Vgs, therefore exp(qVgs/ηkT) changes by 10 for every η x 60 mV ... η x 60 mV is called the subthreshold swing" (section 7.2 "Subthreshold Current - 'Off' Is Not Totally 'Off'")

el.ss-80c.statement: The swing scales with absolute temperature: the 59.5 mV/decade limit at 300 K is 70 mV at the card's 80 °C, and N7's 65 becomes about 77, one reason leakage climbs when the chip is hot.
el.ss-80c.source: C. Hu eq. 7.2.6 (S proportional to T) with n7.ss and NIST k, e
el.ss-80c.note: Leakage also rises because the threshold voltage drops with temperature (generic); the measured total doubles every 25 °C (et.leak-double).

el.finfet-why.statement: Why fins: a thin body with gates on several sides leaves no leakage path far from a gate, so the gate holds the channel shut better and transistors can be shorter, leak less and drive more.
el.finfet-why.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 7 (author's free chapter)
el.finfet-why.quote: "very thin so that no leakage path is far from one of the gates ... For these reasons, a multigate MOSFET can have shorter Lg, lower Ioff, and larger Ion than a single-gate MOSFET." / "A tall FinFET has the advantage of providing a large W and therefore large Ion while occupying a small footprint."

el.dynamic.statement: Every switching cycle moves a charge C x Vdd from the supply into a node and dumps it to ground: dynamic power = k C Vdd² f. Halving the voltage quarters the energy per switch; this is the whole of Esperanto's low-voltage argument.
el.dynamic.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 6 (author's free chapter)
el.dynamic.quote: "In each switching cycle, a charge CVdd is transferred from the power supply to the load, C. ... P_dynamic = Vdd x average current = kCVdd^2 f ... Power consumption can be reduced by lowering Vdd and by minimizing all capacitances"

el.kt.statement: Thermal energy kT is 25.9 meV at room temperature (30.4 meV at 80 °C): the band gap is about 43 kT, so thermal agitation alone frees almost no electrons; the dopants' 50 meV is only 2 kT, so they are all ionised.

el.electron.statement: The charge of one electron is 1.602176634 x 10^-19 C (exact by definition), so 1 fC is 6,242 electrons.

el.channel-electrons.statement: When a single fin is on at the minion's 0.517 V, its channel holds only about 85-120 electrons (with an assumed 0.3 V threshold); at N7's nominal 0.75 V, about 180-250.
el.channel-electrons.source: arithmetic on gate.cap-fin, et.v-minion and an assumed threshold
el.channel-electrons.note: Vt of 0.3 V is an assumption (n7.vt-abs is unknown); the count is a gate-oxide-capacitor estimate, ignoring quantum and fringe effects.

el.sram-node.statement: A 6T SRAM bit is held as a voltage on two tiny nodes. Each node is roughly 0.1-0.3 fF (the gates of the other inverter's two 1-fin transistors plus three drains and a few tens of nanometres of wire); at the 0.705 V SRAM rail that is about 440-1,300 electrons, roughly a thousand.
el.sram-node.note: No source publishes an N7 storage-node capacitance; the range is built from two fin gates (~0.13-0.18 fF) plus drain and wire capacitance. The cross-coupled inverters keep restoring it, so it needs no refresh (memory-levels l2:l2.seq.no-refresh.01). In the minion's latch arrays at 0.517 V the same capacitance holds about 320-970 electrons.

el.dram-cell.statement: A DRAM bit is charge on one capacitor: modern cells (2019-2022 generations) are under 10 fF, heading to 6-7. At about 1-1.1 V that is roughly 45,000-70,000 electrons for a full cell; the sense amplifier sees half of that against the half-voltage bitline.
el.dram-cell.source: arithmetic on TechInsights' cell capacitance and the LPDDR4X array voltage (assumed about VDD2 = 1.1 V)
el.dram-cell.note: The card's LPDDR4X die (Micron) and its generation are not known (memory-levels dram.org.part); the array voltage is an assumption. A DRAM cell holds about 50 times more electrons than an SRAM node, because it has no circuit to restore it and must survive 32 ms between refreshes.
el.dram-cell.quote: TechInsights: "D1z and D1a cell capacitances are now lower than 10 fF/cell". Q = 7-10 fF x 1.0-1.1 V = 7-11 fC = 44,000-69,000 electrons

el.dram-leak.statement: To lose no more than a tenth of 60,000 electrons in a 32 ms refresh window a DRAM cell may leak only about 190,000 electrons a second: 30 femtoamps, about 50,000 times less than the average transistor's leakage on this chip.
el.dram-leak.source: arithmetic on el.dram-cell, the JEDEC LPDDR4 32 ms refresh window (memory-levels dram:gen.refresh) and et.leak-per-tr
el.dram-leak.note: The tenth is an illustrative margin, not a JEDEC figure.

el.bus-bit.statement: Toggling one operand-word bit outside the tensor unit costs 15.5 fJ: an effective 58 fF of wire and drivers at 0.517 V, about 190,000 electrons; wires, not transistors, hold most of the switched charge.
el.bus-bit.note: Same E = C V^2 convention as et.flip-reg; a toggle that only discharges draws nothing from the supply, so this is an upper bound on C.

wire.cu.statement: Copper is face-centred cubic, 0.3615 nm cube, resistivity 16.78 nΩ·m in bulk: a 20 nm-wide M0-M4 wire is about 78 copper atoms across, thin enough that surface scattering raises its resistance well above bulk.
wire.cu.note: 78 atoms: 20 nm / (0.3615/sqrt 2 = 0.256 nm nearest-neighbour distance) (derived); the size-effect remark is generic.

p.atom.1.statement: Silicon has 14 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 4 in the third (ground configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p2).
p.atom.1.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026)

p.atom.2.statement: Removing the outer four electrons one at a time costs 8.15, 16.35, 33.49 and 45.14 eV; the fifth, the first of the inner ten, costs 166.8 eV, and the last (1s) electron 2,673 eV.
p.atom.2.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026)

p.atom.3.statement: The four outer (valence) electrons each pair with an electron of a neighbouring atom: four covalent bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, which is what builds the diamond-cubic crystal.
p.atom.3.source: S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)

p.atom.4.statement: In the crystal neighbouring atoms are 0.235 nm apart, and there are 49.9 atoms in every cubic nanometre (5.0 x 10^22 per cm3).
p.atom.4.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)
p.atom.4.note: sqrt(3)/4 x 0.5431 nm = 0.2352 nm; 8 atoms per cubic cell / (0.5431 nm)^3 = 49.9 per nm^3

p.atom.5.statement: Breaking the crystal into free atoms costs 4.63 eV per atom: about 2.3 eV per bond, since each atom shares four bonds and each bond has two ends.
p.atom.5.source: C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (Wiley, 2005), ch. 3, Table 1 (cohesive energies): Si 4.63 eV per atom

p.atom.6.statement: Natural silicon is 92.22% silicon-28, 4.69% silicon-29 and 3.09% silicon-30; its standard atomic weight is 28.084-28.086.
p.atom.6.source: NIST, Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for Silicon, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/Compositions/stand_alone.pl?ele=Si (read 1 Oct 2026)

p.atom.7.statement: Band gap 1.12 eV at 300 K: an electron needs that much energy to leave its bond and move freely. The thermal energy kT at 300 K is 25.85 meV, 43 times smaller.
p.atom.7.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others; NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)
p.atom.7.note: kT derived from the Boltzmann constant (exact)

p.atom.8.statement: So pure silicon at room temperature has only about 10^10 free electrons per cm3: one for every 5 x 10^12 atoms.
p.atom.8.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others; NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.atom.9.statement: A FinFET channel of about 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm holds about 257,000 silicon atoms and, on average, 5 x 10^-8 thermally freed electrons: none. The transistor conducts only when the gate voltage pulls electrons in from the heavily doped source.
p.atom.9.source: the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si); Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others
p.atom.9.note: the channel's size is the chip page's inference (TSMC does not publish N7's); the conduction picture is the textbook MOSFET (Sze ch. 6)

p.atom.10.statement: With more than 24 billion transistors and about 257,000 atoms per fin's channel, the chip's channels hold at least 6 x 10^15 silicon atoms: about 0.3 micrograms if each transistor has one fin, about a microgram if three. That is all the silicon that actually switches.
p.atom.10.source: the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si); docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/facts.json (chip.process): TSMC 7 nm, more than 24 billion transistors (Esperanto, Hot Chips 33 and IEEE Micro 2022)
p.atom.10.note: the transistor count is Esperanto's; fins per transistor and N7's channel size are not published, so this is an order of magnitude

p.atom.11.statement: Its share of the crystal (a sphere of radius 118 pm) is about 32,000 times wider than its nucleus.
p.atom.11.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm
p.atom.11.note: a sphere of radius 117.6 pm (half the 0.2352 nm neighbour distance) against the nucleus's 3.64 fm radius (1.2 fm x 28^(1/3)): 117.6 / 0.00364 = 32,300

p.dopant.1.statement: Phosphorus and arsenic are donors in silicon: the spare electron is held by only 0.045 eV (P) or 0.054 eV (As). Boron is an acceptor, at 0.045 eV.
p.dopant.1.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others

p.dopant.2.statement: Those energies are only about 2 kT at room temperature (2 kT = 52 meV), so nearly every dopant atom has given up (or taken) its electron.
p.dopant.2.source: S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors); NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.dopant.3.statement: In a TSMC FinFET patent, the n-type source/drain is epitaxial silicon or silicon carbide with phosphorus (Si:P, SiCP), which pulls the channel under tension; the p-type source/drain is silicon-germanium (10-40% germanium in the first layer, 20-80% in the second) doped with boron (5 x 10^20 to 10^22 per cm3 in the second layer), which squeezes the channel.
p.dopant.3.source: TSMC, US Patent 11,107,923 B2, "Source/drain regions of FinFET devices and methods of forming same" (priority 14 Jun 2019), description (a patent's embodiments, not a statement about N7)
p.dopant.3.note: a patent's embodiments; TSMC does not say which apply to N7. Tension speeds electrons and compression speeds holes.

p.dopant.4.statement: TSMC's IEDM 2016 7 nm paper describes epitaxially raised sources and drains that strain the channel, and a contact structure designed to reduce resistance.
p.dopant.4.source: C. Edwards, "7nm finFET process techniques lead IEDM lineup", Tech Design Forums, 24 Oct 2016 (on S.-Y. Wu et al., TSMC, IEDM 2016 paper 2.6)

p.dopant.5.statement: 10^21 dopant atoms per cm3 is one per cubic nanometre, among 50 silicon atoms: about 1 atom in 50. At 10^22, one in 5.
p.dopant.5.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)
p.dopant.5.note: 10^21 per cm^3 = 1 per nm^3; silicon has 49.9 atoms per nm^3 (p.atom.4)

p.dopant.6.statement: So much doping is needed at the contacts: a metal on lightly doped silicon forms a barrier (a Schottky barrier); heavy doping makes it thin enough for electrons to tunnel through. For 7 nm-class technology a contact resistivity below 2 x 10^-9 ohm cm2 is the stated goal.
p.dopant.6.source: IBM, US Patent 10,431,502 B1, "Maskless epitaxial growth of phosphorus-doped Si and boron-doped SiGe (Ge) for advanced source/drain contact" (priority 16 Apr 2018), background; S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)

p.dopant.7.statement: The same patent dopes the wells under the fins at 10^16 to 10^18 per cm3. At those levels a 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm channel would hold on average 0.05 to 5.1 dopant atoms, among some 257,000 silicon atoms: a handful at most, and their random number and place would make every transistor different. FinFET channels are therefore left nearly undoped and the threshold voltage is set by the gate metal instead.
p.dopant.7.source: TSMC, US Patent 11,107,923 B2, "Source/drain regions of FinFET devices and methods of forming same" (priority 14 Jun 2019), description (a patent's embodiments, not a statement about N7); the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si); S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)
p.dopant.7.note: whether N7 dopes its channels, and how much, is not published (unknown); the count is arithmetic on an inferred volume and the patent's well range

p.core.1.statement: The 1s pair sits about 3.9 pm from the nucleus and the 2s and 2p eight about 21 pm: the outer four, around 118 pm, are some 5 to 30 times farther out.
p.core.1.source: E. Clementi and D. L. Raimondi, "Atomic screening constants from SCF functions", J. Chem. Phys. 38, 2686 (1963): Si Zeff 1s 13.575, 2p 9.945 (as tabulated in Wikipedia, "Effective nuclear charge"); NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)
p.core.1.note: hydrogen-like estimate with effective nuclear charges; good for the nodeless 1s and 2p orbitals

p.core.2.statement: The 1s electrons feel almost the full nuclear charge (an effective 13.6 of 14); the 3p electrons feel only 4.3, because the inner ten stand in between.
p.core.2.source: E. Clementi and D. L. Raimondi, "Atomic screening constants from SCF functions", J. Chem. Phys. 38, 2686 (1963): Si Zeff 1s 13.575, 2p 9.945 (as tabulated in Wikipedia, "Effective nuclear charge")

p.core.3.statement: The innermost electron of a silicon atom is bound by 2,673 eV, more than 300 times an outer electron's 8.15 eV.
p.core.3.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026)

p.core.4.statement: An electron in an atom is not a little ball on an orbit: the shells are clouds of probability, and the radii here are where each cloud is densest.
p.core.4.source: S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)

p.nucleus.1.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

p.nucleus.2.statement: Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm: for A = 28, R = 3.64 fm, about 7.3 fm across.
p.nucleus.2.source: K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm

p.nucleus.3.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

p.nucleus.4.statement: The nucleus holds 99.97% of the atom's mass; the 14 electrons, 0.027%.
p.nucleus.4.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021)); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

p.nucleus.5.statement: Its density is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg per m3: a teaspoon (5 mL) of nuclear matter would weigh about 1.1 billion tonnes.
p.nucleus.5.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021)); K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm

p.nucleus.6.statement: If the nucleus were a 1 cm marble, the atom's share of the crystal would be about 320 m across: an atom is almost all empty space.
p.nucleus.6.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm
p.nucleus.6.note: the 32,000 ratio of p.atom.11 applied to a 1 cm marble: 1 cm x 32,300 = 323 m

p.nucleus.7.statement: Binding energy 8.448 MeV per nucleon, 237 MeV in all: the nucleus weighs 0.9% less than its 28 separate parts (E = mc^2).
p.nucleus.7.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

p.nucleus.8.statement: That is about a million times the energy of the outer electrons (8.15 eV) or of a chemical bond (about 2.3 eV): why chemistry, and electronics, never change a nucleus.
p.nucleus.8.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021)); NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026); C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (Wiley, 2005), ch. 3, Table 1 (cohesive energies): Si 4.63 eV per atom

p.nucleon.1.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

p.nucleon.2.statement: Older electron-scattering measurements gave about 0.88 fm; muonic-hydrogen spectroscopy gave 0.84 fm, the 'proton radius puzzle'. The Particle Data Group still notes that the two kinds of measurement are not averaged.
p.nucleon.2.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

p.nucleon.3.statement: Proton mass 938.272 MeV/c^2, neutron 939.565 MeV/c^2: each about 1836 times an electron's.
p.nucleon.3.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

p.nucleon.4.statement: Quark content: proton uud, neutron udd. Charges +2/3 e for up and -1/3 e for down give +1 and 0.
p.nucleon.4.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: quarks (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-quarks.pdf)

p.nucleon.5.statement: A free neutron decays in 878.3 +/- 0.4 s on average; bound in silicon-28 it is stable.
p.nucleon.5.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

p.nucleon.6.statement: The neutron has no charge, but its charge is spread unevenly: its mean-square charge radius is negative (-0.1155 fm^2), meaning a positive core and a negative outer part.
p.nucleon.6.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

p.nucleon.7.statement: No proton has ever been seen to decay: its lifetime exceeds 2.4 x 10^34 years for the decay to a positron and a pion (the universe is 1.4 x 10^10 years old).
p.nucleon.7.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1

p.nucleon.8.statement: Each silicon-28 atom holds 42 up and 42 down quarks (84 in all); a 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm channel's ~257,000 atoms hold some 22 million quarks and 3.6 million electrons.
p.nucleon.8.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si)
p.nucleon.8.note: the per-atom count is arithmetic (derived); the channel count rests on the inferred channel size

p.quark.1.statement: Upper limit on the effective quark radius: 4.3 x 10^-19 m (95% confidence), from electron-proton collisions at HERA.
p.quark.1.source: ZEUS Collaboration, "Limits on the effective quark radius from inclusive ep scattering at HERA", Phys. Lett. B 757, 468 (2016), arXiv:1604.01280

p.quark.2.statement: The proton is at least 1,955 times wider than a quark could be.
