p.quark.2.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); ZEUS Collaboration, "Limits on the effective quark radius from inclusive ep scattering at HERA", Phys. Lett. B 757, 468 (2016), arXiv:1604.01280

p.quark.3.statement: Masses (MS-bar at 2 GeV): up 2.16 +/- 0.07 MeV, down 4.70 +/- 0.07 MeV. Two ups and a down add to 9.0 MeV: 1% of the proton's 938.3 MeV.
p.quark.3.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: quarks (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-quarks.pdf); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)
p.quark.3.note: quark masses depend on the scheme and scale they are quoted at; the simple sum is an illustration

p.quark.4.statement: A lattice-QCD breakdown of the proton's mass: the quarks' masses (through the quark condensate, u, d and s) give 9%, the quarks' energy of motion 33%, the gluon field's energy 37%, and the 'trace anomaly' 23%.
p.quark.4.source: Y.-B. Yang et al. (chiQCD), "Proton mass decomposition from the QCD energy momentum tensor", Phys. Rev. Lett. 121, 212001 (2018), arXiv:1808.08677

p.quark.5.statement: Lattice QCD computes the proton's and neutron's masses from the quark and gluon theory, matching experiment.
p.quark.5.source: S. Duerr et al., "Ab initio determination of light hadron masses", Science 322, 1224 (2008), arXiv:0906.3599

p.quark.6.statement: Gluons carry the strong force between quarks; they are massless in theory (a mass of a few MeV is not excluded) and come in eight colour states.
p.quark.6.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: gauge and Higgs bosons, gluon (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-gauge-higgs-bosons.pdf); Particle Data Group (2026), review 15, Quark Model (C. Amsler, V. Crede et al., rev. Aug 2025), sec. 15.1-15.2

p.quark.7.statement: Colour is believed to be permanently confined: only colourless combinations (three quarks, or a quark and an antiquark) exist on their own.
p.quark.7.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 15, Quark Model (C. Amsler, V. Crede et al., rev. Aug 2025), sec. 15.1-15.2

p.quark.8.statement: Squeezing quarks into 0.84 fm gives them energies around hbar c / r = 235 MeV each: why most of a proton's mass is energy rather than quark mass.
p.quark.8.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)
p.quark.8.note: an uncertainty-principle estimate, order of magnitude only

p.electron.1.statement: Charge -1.602176634 x 10^-19 C, exactly (it defines the coulomb since 2019); mass 9.1094 x 10^-31 kg = 0.51100 MeV/c^2.
p.electron.1.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.electron.2.statement: A radius limit below 2 x 10^-20 m, from contact-interaction searches at LEP at the 10 TeV scale.
p.electron.2.source: G. Gabrielse group (Northwestern Center for Fundamental Physics), "Limit on Electron Substructure", cfp.physics.northwestern.edu/gabrielse-group/electron-substructure.html, citing D. Bourilkov, Phys. Rev. D 64, 071701(R) (2001) for the LEP contact-interaction limit

p.electron.3.statement: Its magnetic moment is measured to about 1 part in 10^13 ((g-2)/2 = 0.00115965218062(12)) and agrees with the theory of a point particle; an electron made of smaller parts would spoil that agreement.
p.electron.3.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf); G. Gabrielse group (Northwestern Center for Fundamental Physics), "Limit on Electron Substructure", cfp.physics.northwestern.edu/gabrielse-group/electron-substructure.html, citing D. Bourilkov, Phys. Rev. D 64, 071701(R) (2001) for the LEP contact-interaction limit

p.electron.4.statement: The electron is round: its electric dipole moment is below 4.1 x 10^-30 e cm (PDG 2026), so its charge sits within 4.1 x 10^-32 m of its centre (dipole moment divided by its charge).
p.electron.4.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)
p.electron.4.note: the dipole limit divided by the charge: 4.1 x 10^-30 e cm / e = 4.1 x 10^-30 cm = 4.1 x 10^-32 m

p.electron.5.statement: The 'classical electron radius', 2.818 fm, is a length built from its charge and mass, not its size.
p.electron.5.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.electron.6.statement: Stable: its lifetime exceeds 6.6 x 10^28 years.
p.electron.6.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

p.electron.7.statement: Every coulomb that flows through the chip is 6.24 x 10^18 electrons.
p.electron.7.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.planck.1.statement: Planck length 1.616255 x 10^-35 m; Planck time 5.391247 x 10^-44 s.
p.planck.1.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.planck.2.statement: Max Planck introduced these natural units of length, mass, time and temperature in 1899.
p.planck.2.source: M. Planck, "Ueber irreversible Strahlungsvorgaenge", Sitzungsberichte der Koeniglich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin (1899), pp. 440-480 (natural units of length, mass, time and temperature)

p.planck.3.statement: The quark's radius limit is 3 x 10^16 times the Planck length: some 16 powers of ten that no experiment has probed.
p.planck.3.source: ZEUS Collaboration, "Limits on the effective quark radius from inclusive ep scattering at HERA", Phys. Lett. B 757, 468 (2016), arXiv:1604.01280; NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

p.planck.4.statement: Whether the Planck length is a smallest possible length is an open question: thought experiments and several approaches to quantum gravity suggest a minimal length, and none is confirmed.
p.planck.4.source: S. Hossenfelder, "Minimal length scale scenarios for quantum gravity", Living Rev. Relativ. 16, 2 (2013), arXiv:1203.6191

p.planck.5.statement: From the Planck length to the observable universe's diameter is 61.7 powers of ten.
p.planck.5.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)

p.wrap.1.statement: Joel Primack and Nancy Ellen Abrams, adapting an idea of Sheldon Glashow (Nobel 1979), drew the 'Cosmic Uroboros': the tip of the tail is the Planck length, the head is the cosmic horizon, about 60 powers of ten apart.
p.wrap.1.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf); S. L. Glashow's cosmic uroboros, as credited by Primack and Abrams (ch. 6, note 4): first version reproduced in T. Ferris, New York Times Magazine, 26 Sep 1982, p. 38; see also S. L. Glashow with B. Bova, Interactions (Warner Books, 1988), ch. 14 (not read directly)

p.wrap.2.statement: Their first meaning: gravity, negligible from bacteria to atoms, becomes strong again at the tail's tip, so it may link the largest and smallest sizes (a hope of quantum gravity and string theory, not yet tested).
p.wrap.2.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)

p.wrap.3.statement: Their second meaning: at the very beginning of the Big Bang the largest scale, the horizon, was not much larger than the smallest; the serpent's body filled in as the universe expanded.
p.wrap.3.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)
p.wrap.3.note: the horizon's growth from near-Planck size rests on extrapolating known physics back to the Planck time

p.wrap.4.statement: Looking out is looking back: the farthest light we can see, the cosmic microwave background, left 380,000 years after the Big Bang; before that the universe was hot, dense and opaque.
p.wrap.4.source: NASA Science, Physics of the Cosmos, "Big Bang and the Evolution of the Universe", science.nasa.gov/astrophysics/programs/physics-of-the-cosmos/big-bang-and-the-evolution-of-the-universe/ (read 1 Oct 2026); NASA Science, "Cosmic History", science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (read 1 Oct 2026)

p.wrap.5.statement: The early universe is 'the poor man's accelerator' (Zel'dovich): its first minutes reached energies that test particle physics.
p.wrap.5.source: G. Leconte-Chevillard, "'The poor man's accelerator', or how the primordial universe became a testing ground for particle physics", Synthese 207 (2026), doi:10.1007/s11229-026-05476-2

p.wrap.6.statement: Example: the helium made in the first three minutes limited how many kinds of neutrino could exist (Steigman, Schramm and Gunn, 1977); collider measurements of the Z boson later counted 2.996 +/- 0.007.
p.wrap.6.source: G. Steigman, D. N. Schramm, J. E. Gunn, "Cosmological limits to the number of massive leptons", Phys. Lett. B 66, 202 (1977); G. Leconte-Chevillard, "'The poor man's accelerator', or how the primordial universe became a testing ground for particle physics", Synthese 207 (2026), doi:10.1007/s11229-026-05476-2; Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

p.wrap.7.statement: On a logarithmic scale the middle of the whole ladder, between the Planck length and the observable universe, is 0.12 mm: about the size of a minion's 4 KB L1 data cache or one SRAM panel of the shire cache in this chip.
p.wrap.7.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond); the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si)
p.wrap.7.note: the two chip sizes are the chip page's order-of-magnitude inferences

p.wrap.8.statement: Primack and Abrams place human size near the centre of the uroboros, with their round numbers (10^-33 cm to 10^28 cm).
p.wrap.8.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)

e.cmb.1.statement: Last scattering at redshift z* = 1089.92 +/- 0.25, age 372.6 +/- 1.0 thousand years (Planck 2018 base model).
e.cmb.1.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; Planck Collaboration, "Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters", A&A 641, A6 (2020)

e.cmb.2.statement: Then the universe was 1 + z* = 1091 times hotter than the CMB's 2.7255 K today: 2,973 K, cool enough for electrons and nuclei to form atoms.
e.cmb.2.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; D. J. Fixsen, "The temperature of the cosmic microwave background", ApJ 707, 916 (2009); NASA Science, "Cosmic History", science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (read 1 Oct 2026)

e.cmb.3.statement: The region that is now our observable universe was then 85 million light-years across.
e.cmb.3.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
e.cmb.3.note: today's comoving diameter divided by 1 + z*

e.cmb.4.statement: Its temperature varied by about 1 part in 100,000 from place to place (COBE): the seeds that grew into galaxies.
e.cmb.4.source: NASA Science, "COBE's Top Discoveries", science.nasa.gov/mission/cobe/science/ (read 1 Oct 2026); NASA Science, "Cosmic History", science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (read 1 Oct 2026)

e.cmb.5.statement: That light is still all around: about 411 CMB photons in every cubic centimetre of space, at 2.7255 K.
e.cmb.5.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; D. J. Fixsen, "The temperature of the cosmic microwave background", ApJ 707, 916 (2009)

e.cmb.6.statement: In the leading theory, inflation, those seeds began as quantum fluctuations on sub-atomic scales, stretched to the size of galaxies: the smallest scales shaping the largest. Planck's measurements fit simple inflation models; inflation is not proven.
e.cmb.6.source: Planck Collaboration, "Planck 2018 results. X. Constraints on inflation", A&A 641, A10 (2020), arXiv:1807.06211

e.bbn.1.statement: Deuterium, helium-3, helium-4 and lithium-7 were made at the end of the first three minutes, once the temperature fell to about 0.1 MeV (1.2 billion K); nuclear reactions were fixed by about 180 s.
e.bbn.1.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

e.bbn.2.statement: Primordial helium is 24.5% of the ordinary matter by mass (Yp = 0.2448 +/- 0.0033). No silicon was made: nuclei heavier than lithium do not form in significant amounts.
e.bbn.2.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

e.bbn.3.statement: The region that is now our observable universe was then about 200 light-years across.
e.bbn.3.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
e.bbn.3.note: entropy conservation, a T g*s^(1/3) constant, with g*s = 3.91 after electron-positron annihilation

e.bbn.4.statement: There are about 1.66 billion CMB photons for every proton or neutron (eta = 6.04 x 10^-10).
e.bbn.4.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

e.bbn.5.statement: The universe holds matter and almost no antimatter: in the standard reading, matter outnumbered antimatter by a tiny margin early on, and the leftover makes every proton and neutron, including the chip's.
e.bbn.5.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2
e.bbn.5.note: the standard reading of the baryon asymmetry (eta) in PDG review 22, sec. 22.3.6; why it arose is the next fact

e.bbn.6.statement: Why there was a margin at all (baryogenesis) is unknown: it needs baryon-number violation, C and CP violation and a departure from equilibrium, and several mechanisms are viable.
e.bbn.6.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis)

e.qcd.1.statement: Above about 156.5 MeV (1.8 x 10^12 K) quarks and gluons are not bound into protons and neutrons: a quark-gluon plasma. Lattice QCD puts the crossover at 156.5 +/- 1.5 MeV.
e.qcd.1.source: A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235; Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis)

e.qcd.2.statement: The universe cooled through it 14-24 microseconds after the Big Bang.
e.qcd.2.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235
e.qcd.2.note: PDG eq. 22.44 with N = 51.25 just above and 17.25 just below the transition

e.qcd.3.statement: The region that is now our observable universe was then about 3,700 to 5,300 times the Earth-Sun distance across (under a tenth of a light-year).
e.qcd.3.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
e.qcd.3.note: entropy conservation (a T g*s^(1/3) constant) from today's 8.74 x 10^26 m, 2.7255 K and g*s = 3.91 back to 156.5 MeV, with g*s between 69/4 (hadrons) and 205/4 (quarks and gluons): 5.6-8.0 x 10^14 m, 3,700-5,300 au

e.qcd.4.statement: At that temperature a typical particle's wavelength, hbar c / kT = 1.26 fm, is the size of a proton: the universe's 'microscope' and the proton's size meet.
e.qcd.4.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235; Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

e.qcd.5.statement: The protons and neutrons in the chip's nuclei first formed in this transition; billions of years later, stars built them into silicon.
e.qcd.5.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); J. A. Johnson, "Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements", Science 363, 474 (2019)
e.qcd.5.note: protons and neutrons formed at the QCD crossover (e.qcd.1-2); silicon is made in stars (e.stars.1)

e.qcd.6.statement: The LHC recreates this plasma by colliding lead nuclei, at temperatures more than 100,000 times the centre of the Sun.
e.qcd.6.source: CERN press release, "Quark Matter 2017: understanding the early universe", 9 Feb 2017, home.cern

e.ew.1.statement: The Standard Model's electroweak crossover, when the Higgs field takes its value, is at 159.5 +/- 1.5 GeV (lattice).
e.ew.1.source: M. D'Onofrio and K. Rummukainen, "Standard model cross-over on the lattice", Phys. Rev. D 93, 025003 (2016), arXiv:1508.07161

e.ew.2.statement: That was about 9 picoseconds after the Big Bang, when the region that is now our observable universe was about 3 times the Earth-Sun distance across.
e.ew.2.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); M. D'Onofrio and K. Rummukainen, "Standard model cross-over on the lattice", Phys. Rev. D 93, 025003 (2016), arXiv:1508.07161; the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
e.ew.2.note: PDG eq. 22.44 with all Standard Model particles, N = 106.75

e.ew.3.statement: In the Standard Model the electron and the quarks get their masses from the Higgs field. The electron's mass sets the size of every atom (the Bohr radius is inversely proportional to it), and so the size of the chip's transistors.
e.ew.3.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

e.planck.1.statement: Planck time 5.391247 x 10^-44 s: before it, known physics cannot describe the universe.
e.planck.1.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

e.planck.2.statement: What happened at or before the Planck time, and whether 'before' means anything, is unknown.
e.planck.2.source: S. Hossenfelder, "Minimal length scale scenarios for quantum gravity", Living Rev. Relativ. 16, 2 (2013), arXiv:1203.6191

e.stars.1.statement: Silicon is made in massive stars, by oxygen burning late in their lives, and spread by their supernova explosions; exploding white dwarfs make some too.
e.stars.1.source: J. A. Johnson, "Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements", Science 363, 474 (2019); S. E. Woosley, A. Heger, T. A. Weaver, "The evolution and explosion of massive stars", Rev. Mod. Phys. 74, 1015 (2002)

e.stars.2.statement: The Sun and its planets formed from gas already enriched by earlier stars; the oldest solids in the Solar System are 4,567.30 +/- 0.16 million years old.
e.stars.2.source: J. N. Connelly et al., "The absolute chronology and thermal processing of solids in the solar protoplanetary disk", Science 338, 651 (2012); J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)

e.stars.3.statement: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, more than 25% by weight.
e.stars.3.source: L. A. Corathers (USGS), "Mineral resource of the month: silicon", Geotimes (2003), usgs.gov/publications/mineral-resource-month-silicon

e.stars.4.statement: So the silicon atoms in the chip's fins were forged in stars of the Milky Way more than 4.6 billion years ago, from protons and neutrons formed in the first 20 microseconds: a physical link between the ladder's top and bottom.
e.stars.4.source: J. A. Johnson, "Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements", Science 363, 474 (2019); J. N. Connelly et al., "The absolute chronology and thermal processing of solids in the solar protoplanetary disk", Science 338, 651 (2012); A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235
e.stars.4.note: e.stars.1 (silicon from massive stars and supernovae), e.stars.2 (the Solar System from enriched gas, 4,567 million years ago) and e.qcd.5

s45.1.statement: The lab's rack stands in Studio 45, the owner's name for the place, which is on 29th Street in Bernal Heights, San Francisco.

s45.2.statement: Studio 45 is a co-working and event space for people who build physical things: "space, tools, and resources for the hardware community".
s45.2.source: Studio 45's own website and event listings (read 1 Oct 2026; not linked here: their pages give the street address)

s45.3.statement: It has two floors of co-working space, a wood shop, 3D printers, a metal CNC mill, a laser cutter and a 4 x 8 ft three-axis CNC router, with assembly space in a street-level warehouse and courtyard.
s45.3.source: Studio 45's own website and event listings (read 1 Oct 2026; not linked here: their pages give the street address)

s45.4.statement: It opened with a launch party on 9 December 2021, as "San Francisco's newest co-working space for people who make real things for a living".
s45.4.source: SF Station, event listing "Studio 45 Launch" (9 Dec 2021; not linked here: it gives the street address)

s45.5.statement: It describes itself as a coworking space for the hardware community "at the intersection of The Mission and Bernal Heights", and hosts the monthly SF Hardware Meetup.
s45.5.source: SF Hardware Meetup event listings (2025-2026; not linked here: they give the street address)

s45.6.statement: The building at its address is about 37 m deep and 9 m wide (325 m² on the ground) and 6 to 8 m tall: two storeys.
s45.6.source: City and County of San Francisco, DataSF (Open Data Commons PDDL), Building Footprints (ynuv-fyni; a 2010 3D model split at parcel lines)
s45.6.note: Length and width of the footprint polygon and its roof heights (median 6.0 m, highest 8.3 m), read by the venue's public address; only these dimensions were kept. The courtyard and event spaces may reach onto neighbouring lots. Where in the building the rack stands is not recorded.

s45.7.statement: Light crosses the building's 37 m in 123 ns: 74 ticks of the chip's 600 MHz clock.
s45.7.source: the building's length (s45.6) divided by the speed of light; the 600 MHz clock of the lab's cards

s45.8.statement: A 4 x 8 ft CNC router cuts a 1.22 x 2.44 m sheet: the size of the bed drawn here.
s45.8.source: the venue's "4'x8' 3-axis CNC with a tool changer" (s45.3) in metres

b.1.statement: Bernal Heights is a residential hill neighbourhood in south-eastern San Francisco, south of the Mission, bounded by Cesar Chavez Street (north), San Jose Avenue (west), US 101 (east) and I-280 (south).
b.1.source: Wikipedia, "Bernal Heights, San Francisco" (read 1 Oct 2026, citing UCSC Critical Sustainabilities); SF Chronicle, 29 Aug 2021

b.2.statement: Its area is 2.79 km², 2.3% of the city's land, about 2.2 km east to west and 2.0 km north to south.
b.2.source: City and County of San Francisco, DataSF (Open Data Commons PDDL), Analysis Neighborhoods (j2bu-swwd)
b.2.note: Area and extent of the "Bernal Heights" polygon on the San Francisco map's projection (equirectangular at 37.76 N); 2.79 / 121.51 km² of land = 2.3%.

b.3.statement: About 26,140 people live there (2012-2016), some 3% of the city.
b.3.source: SF Planning, "San Francisco Neighborhoods: Socio-Economic Profiles, American Community Survey 2012-2016" (Sept 2018), p. 10
b.3.note: 26,140 of 873,965 (2020 census) is 3.0%. Wikipedia gives 25,125 for 2019 (city-data.com).

b.4.statement: The hill's summit is 142 m (466 ft) above sea level, about half the height of Mount Davidson, the city's highest point (283 m).
b.4.source: USGS 3DEP 1 m lidar elevation model (flown 4 Mar 2023, NAVD88) through the USGS Elevation Point Query Service; SF Planning, Conditional Use Authorization 2010.0306C (466 ft)
b.4.note: The highest ground within 80 m of the GNIS summit point (GNIS 1658039): 141.99 m. Other published values: 433 ft (1958) and "475+ ft" (USGS 7.5' topo, NGVD29).

b.5.statement: Bernal Heights Park covers the hilltop: 26.3 acres (10.7 ha), with a 50-foot telecommunications tower at the top.
b.5.source: City and County of San Francisco, DataSF (Open Data Commons PDDL), Recreation and Parks Properties (gtr9-ntp6); Wikipedia, "Bernal Heights Summit" (SF Planning)

b.6.statement: The hill is folded layers of red radiolarian chert: microcrystalline quartz, silicon dioxide, made from the silica shells of plankton 0.5 to 1.5 mm across that settled on the deep-sea floor 200 to 100 million years ago.
b.6.source: National Park Service, Golden Gate National Recreation Area, "Chert FAQ"; Wikipedia, "Bernal Heights Summit" and "Chert"

b.7.statement: Silicon for chips is refined from silica, silicon dioxide like the hill's quartz: reduced to silicon metal, then purified into the "ultra-high-purity" polysilicon of semiconductor grade.

b.8.statement: Light crosses the neighbourhood's 2.2 km in 7.3 µs: 4,403 ticks of the chip's clock.
b.8.source: the neighbourhood's width (b.2) divided by the speed of light; the cards' 600 MHz clock

b.9.statement: It is named after José Cornelio Bernal, who received the Rancho Rincon de las Salinas y Potrero Viejo land grant in 1839.

st.1.statement: 29th Street is 1.29 km long. It runs east from Diamond Street, at the foot of Diamond Heights, through Noe Valley to Mission Street, where the Mission meets Bernal Heights.
st.1.source: City and County of San Francisco, DataSF (Open Data Commons PDDL), Streets - Active and Retired (3psu-pn9h, Public Works centrelines)
st.1.note: The sum of its nine centreline segments: 1,293 m. (Not 29th Avenue, in the Richmond and Sunset.)

st.2.statement: It falls about 95 m along its length, from 126 m above sea level at Diamond Street to about 30 m at its east end; the steepest part is the top, 34 m down in the first 140 m (about 24%).
st.2.source: USGS 3DEP 1 m lidar elevation model through the Elevation Point Query Service, sampled every 40 m along the street
st.2.note: research/epqs_29th.out: 28 samples, distances and heights only

st.3.statement: Light runs the street's length in 4.31 µs: 2,588 ticks of the chip's clock.
st.3.source: the street's length (st.1) divided by the speed of light; the cards' 600 MHz clock

tb.gates.statement: A static CMOS gate pairs a pull-up network of PMOS transistors with a complementary pull-down network of NMOS transistors: a NOR has its PMOS in series and its NMOS in parallel, a NAND the reverse, and a compound gate such as AND-OR-INVERT combines series and parallel transistors in one stage.
tb.gates.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 1 (CMOS logic) and ch. 9 (combinational circuits)

tb.prefix.statement: A parallel-prefix adder computes for each bit a generate g = a·b and a propagate p = a XOR b, combines them in a tree of carry cells (G = Gi + Pi·Gj, P = Pi·Pj) of log2 n levels, and forms each sum bit as p XOR the carry into it; a ripple-carry adder instead passes the carry through all n bits one after another.
tb.prefix.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11 (addition: tree adders); I. Koren, Computer Arithmetic Algorithms, 2nd ed. (A K Peters, 2002), ch. 5

tb.kogge.statement: In the Kogge-Stone prefix tree, level k combines every position with the one 2^k places below it, so that n bits need log2 n levels, each cell driving at most two others.
tb.kogge.source: P. M. Kogge and H. S. Stone, "A Parallel Algorithm for the Efficient Solution of a General Class of Recurrence Equations", IEEE Transactions on Computers C-22(8), 1973, pp. 786-793; N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11

tb.shifter.statement: A logarithmic (barrel) shifter shifts n bits by any amount in log2 n stages: stage k is a row of 2:1 multiplexers, one per bit, that pass each bit straight on or take the bit 2^k places away, as bit k of the shift amount says.
tb.shifter.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11 (shifters)

tb.booth.statement: Radix-4 (modified) Booth recoding looks at overlapping triples of multiplier bits (bits 2i+1, 2i and 2i-1) and makes each partial product 0, +X, +2X, -X or -2X, halving the number of partial products to add; each bit of a partial product is a multiplexer choosing x(j) or x(j-1), followed by an XOR with the sign.
tb.booth.source: A. D. Booth, "A Signed Binary Multiplication Technique", Quarterly Journal of Mechanics and Applied Mathematics 4(2), 1951; O. L. MacSorley, "High-Speed Arithmetic in Binary Computers", Proceedings of the IRE 49(1), 1961; I. Koren, Computer Arithmetic Algorithms, 2nd ed. (A K Peters, 2002), ch. 6; N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11 (multiplication)

tb.booth.table.statement: The radix-4 Booth table: multiplier bits 000 give 0, 001 and 010 give +X, 011 gives +2X, 100 gives -2X, 101 and 110 give -X, and 111 gives 0.
tb.booth.table.source: I. Koren, Computer Arithmetic Algorithms, 2nd ed. (A K Peters, 2002), ch. 6; N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11

tb.lzd.statement: A leading-zero counter for n bits is a tree of log2 n levels: each leaf takes two bits, and each node takes the count of its left half if that half holds a 1, else the count of its right half with one more bit set.
tb.lzd.source: V. G. Oklobdzija, "An Algorithmic and Novel Design of a Leading Zero Detector Circuit: Comparison with Logic Synthesis", IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems 2(1), 1994, pp. 124-128

tb.lza.statement: A leading-zero anticipator predicts the normalisation shift of a floating-point sum from the adder's operands, in parallel with the addition; its prediction can be one position off, which a final one-bit correction fixes.
tb.lza.source: M. S. Schmookler and K. J. Nowka, "Leading Zero Anticipation and Detection: A Comparison of Methods", Proceedings of the 15th IEEE Symposium on Computer Arithmetic (ARITH-15), 2001, pp. 7-12

tb.decoder.statement: An n-to-2^n decoder has one AND gate per output, fed by each address bit or its complement; a memory's row decoder predecodes groups of two or three address bits first and drives each selected row through a buffer.
tb.decoder.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 12 (SRAM row circuitry: decoders)

tb.regfile.statement: A register file keeps each bit in a latch or a multi-ported memory cell; a write decodes its address to enable one row (through a clock gate or a write wordline), and each read port picks one row per bit through a multiplexer tree or a read wordline and bitline.
tb.regfile.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 12 (multiported register files)

tb.icg.statement: An integrated clock gate latches the enable while the clock is high and ANDs it with the clock: a block whose enable is low gets no clock edges, so its flip-flops and clock wires do not switch.
tb.icg.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 10 (sequential circuits) and ch. 5 (power: clock gating)

tb.stdcell.statement: Logic synthesis maps a block's register-transfer-level description onto a library of standard cells (inverters, NAND, NOR, AND-OR-INVERT and XOR gates, multiplexers, flip-flops, clock gates), typically a few hundred kinds of cell of one height, placed in rows.
tb.stdcell.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 14 (design methodology and tools: standard-cell design)

tb.counter.statement: A binary counter is a register and an incrementer: a chain of half adders adds one, each half adder's sum an XOR of its bit and the carry in and its carry an AND of the two.
tb.counter.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11 (counters)

tb.compare.statement: An equality comparator XNORs each pair of bits and combines the results in a tree of NAND and NOR gates: the output is 1 only when every pair agrees.
tb.compare.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11 (comparators)

tb.fifo.statement: A first-in, first-out queue is a small memory addressed by a write pointer and a read pointer, two counters; comparing the pointers tells a full queue from an empty one.
tb.fifo.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 12 (serial-access memories: queues)

tb.pll.statement: A phase-locked loop multiplies a reference clock: a phase-frequency detector compares the reference with the output divided by N, a charge pump and loop filter turn the difference into a control voltage, and a voltage-controlled oscillator, often a ring of an odd number of inverters, settles at N times the reference.
tb.pll.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 13 (clocks: PLLs and DLLs)

tb.ecc.statement: A single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) code adds check bits, each the XOR of a subset of the data bits; recomputed on a read, they give a syndrome that is zero for no error, names the flipped bit for one error and flags two; 64 data bits need 8 check bits, a (72, 64) code.
tb.ecc.source: R. W. Hamming, "Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes", Bell System Technical Journal 29(2), 1950; M. Y. Hsiao, "A Class of Optimal Minimum Odd-Weight-Column SEC-DED Codes", IBM Journal of Research and Development 14(4), 1970; N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 11 (coding)

tb.rom.statement: A NOR ROM stores each bit as a transistor present or absent where a wordline crosses a bitline: the bitlines are precharged high, and when a row rises its transistors pull their bitlines low.
tb.rom.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 12 (read-only memory)

tb.senseamp.statement: A latch-type SRAM sense amplifier is two cross-coupled inverters with a tail NMOS switched by a sense-enable signal: it turns a bitline difference of tens of millivolts into full logic levels; precharge PMOS transistors equalise the bitlines between reads.
tb.senseamp.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 12 (SRAM column circuitry: sense amplifiers); J. Rabaey, A. Chandrakasan and B. Nikolić, Digital Integrated Circuits: A Design Perspective, 2nd ed. (Prentice Hall, 2003), ch. 12

tb.fma.statement: A fused multiply-add computes a x b + c with one rounding: Booth-recoded partial products reduced by a tree of carry-save adders, the addend aligned by a shifter in parallel, one wide addition, a leading-zero count, a normalising shift and a rounding increment.
tb.fma.source: R. K. Montoye, E. Hokenek and S. L. Runyon, "Design of the IBM RISC System/6000 Floating-Point Execution Unit", IBM Journal of Research and Development 34(1), 1990, pp. 59-70; I. Koren, Computer Arithmetic Algorithms, 2nd ed. (A K Peters, 2002), ch. 7

tb.serdes.statement: A serial link's transmitter turns parallel words into one bit stream with a serialiser (a tree of 2:1 multiplexers, each stage at twice the rate of the one before), shapes it with a few-tap FIR equaliser and drives a differential pair of wires; its receiver equalises the attenuated signal (a continuous-time linear equaliser, then a decision-feedback equaliser), samples it with clocked comparators, recovers the clock from the data's own transitions (a phase detector steering a phase interpolator) and deserialises the bits; a PLL makes the fast clock.
tb.serdes.source: N. Weste and D. Harris, CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2011), ch. 13 (I/O and high-speed links); no ET source describes the PHY's circuits

pcie.gen4.eq.statement: PCIe 4.0 at 16 GT/s: the transmitter has a 3-tap feed-forward equaliser (one tap before the bit, one after) with ten presets that the receiver asks for during link training; the reference receiver has a continuous-time linear equaliser with seven settings and a 2-tap decision-feedback equaliser.
pcie.gen4.eq.source: MathWorks, SerDes Toolbox documentation, "PCIe4 Transmitter/Receiver IBIS-AMI Model" (after the PCI Express Base Specification 4.0)

pcie.gen4.loss.statement: A PCIe 4.0 link may lose up to 28 dB at 8 GHz, the Nyquist frequency of a 16 Gb/s signal: up to 20 dB on the system board (5 dB of it in the root complex's package) and 8 dB on the add-in card (3 dB in the endpoint). 28 dB is a signal 25 times weaker in voltage.
pcie.gen4.loss.source: Teledyne LeCroy, "PCIe 4.0 Transmitter Electrical Testing" (blog, 12 January 2018); 10^(28/20) = 25 (arithmetic)

pcie.gen4.ui.statement: At 16 GT/s each bit lasts 62.5 ps (1 / 16 x 10^9 s); 128b/130b coding sends 130 bits for every 128 of data, so one lane carries 1.97 GB/s each way.
pcie.gen4.ui.source: arithmetic on the PCI Express 4.0 rate and coding (in.pcie.phy.3)

tb.strongarm.statement: A clocked comparator (the StrongARM latch) is a sense amplifier: a differential input pair under two cross-coupled inverters; on each clock edge it turns the input difference into a full 0 or 1, drawing no current between decisions. SerDes receivers sample with such latches.
tb.strongarm.source: B. Razavi, "The StrongARM Latch [A Circuit for All Seasons]", IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine 7(2), 2015, pp. 12-17

tb.bangbang.statement: A bang-bang (Alexander) phase detector samples each bit in its middle and at its edge: if the edge sample equals the bit before it the clock is late, if it equals the bit after it the clock is early; XORs of neighbouring samples give each vote, and the votes nudge the sampling clock.
tb.bangbang.source: J. D. H. Alexander, "Clock Recovery from Random Binary Signals", Electronics Letters 11(22), 1975, pp. 541-542

tb.diffpair.statement: A differential pair: two matched transistors whose sources share one tail current source. The input that is higher steers more of the tail current through its own side's load, so the outputs swing with the difference of the two inputs and ignore what the two have in common.
tb.diffpair.source: B. Razavi, Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits, 2nd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2017), ch. 4 (differential amplifiers)

tb.ctle.statement: A continuous-time linear equaliser is a differential pair whose two sources are joined by a resistor and a capacitor in parallel (source degeneration): at low frequencies the resistor cuts the gain, at high frequencies the capacitor shorts it out, so the stage boosts the high frequencies the wire attenuated most. "The most common approach to creating a boost at high frequencies incorporates resistive and capacitive degeneration in a differential pair" (Razavi).
tb.ctle.source: B. Razavi, "The Design of an Equalizer, Part One" (The Analog Mind), IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine 13(4), 2021

tb.xbar.statement: A crossbar switch connects any of its inputs to any output: each output is a multiplexer over all the inputs, its select set each cycle by an arbiter (often round robin, so that every input gets its turn) among the inputs that want that output. Its area is mostly wires: every input crosses every output, each as wide as the datapath.
tb.xbar.source: W. J. Dally and B. Towles, Principles and Practices of Interconnection Networks (Morgan Kaufmann, 2004), ch. 17 (router datapath components: the switch) and ch. 18 (arbitration)

tb.round.statement: Rounding to nearest, ties to even, the default of IEEE 754: of the exact result's bits beyond the last one kept, the first is the guard bit G, the next the round bit R, and the OR of all the rest the sticky bit S. The result rounds up (adds one at the last kept place) when G = 1 and any of R, S or the last kept bit L is 1; a tie (G = 1, R = S = 0) goes to the even neighbour. A carry out of the top shifts the result right by one and adds one to the exponent.
tb.round.source: IEEE Std 754-2019, IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic, §4.3 (rounding-direction attributes; roundTiesToEven the default for binary formats); I. Koren, Computer Arithmetic Algorithms, 2nd ed. (A K Peters, 2002), ch. 4

tb.buck.statement: A buck converter steps a voltage down by switching: a high-side transistor connects an inductor to the input, a low-side one to ground, alternately, hundreds of thousands of times a second; the inductor and the output capacitor average the pulses. In steady state the output is the input times the share of time the high side is on (the duty cycle D = Vout / Vin). A multiphase converter runs several such stages in parallel, their pulses spread through the cycle, to share a large current and cancel ripple.
tb.buck.source: R. W. Erickson and D. Maksimović, Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2020), ch. 2 (principles of steady-state converter analysis: the buck converter)

card.tpsm.statement: The card's core regulator, a Texas Instruments TPSM831D31, is a power module: a D-CAP+ controller with four Smart Power Stages and their inductors in one package, 15 by 48 mm; one output of 3 phases up to 120 A, one of 1 phase up to 40 A, from 8-14 V in, switching at 350-700 kHz.

card.ltm.statement: The card's SRAM-rail regulator, an Analog Devices LTM4680, is a dual 30 A or single 60 A step-down µModule regulator (its switches and inductors inside a 16 x 16 mm package), 4.5-16 V in, 0.5-3.3 V out.
card.ltm.source: Analog Devices, LTM4680 data sheet and product page (analog.com)

buck.duty.statement: Turning the card's 12 V into the minion rail's 0.517 V, a buck converter's high-side switch is on about 4% of each cycle (D = 0.517 / 12 = 0.043): at 500 kHz, about 86 ns of every 2 µs.
buck.duty.source: arithmetic on tb.buck (D = Vout / Vin), out.card.6 (12 V at the card edge) and et.v-minion (0.517 V on die)
buck.duty.note: Losses and the drop between the regulator and the die make the true duty cycle a little higher; 500 kHz is a value inside the TPSM831D31's 350-700 kHz range, not a measured one.

tb.powerfet.statement: A power MOSFET is thousands of small cells in parallel: in a trench-gate device, current flows vertically, from the source on top, down a channel along each trench wall through the p-type body, across a lightly doped drift layer to the heavily doped substrate, the drain, underneath; its on-resistance is milliohms and it blocks tens of volts.
tb.powerfet.source: B. J. Baliga, Fundamentals of Power Semiconductor Devices, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2019), ch. 6 (power MOSFETs)

card.stages.statement: Which transistors the regulators' power stages use is not published in the card's documents.
card.stages.source: Esperanto, "PCIe Dev Card (V3)", ET-PCIe-Dev-Card-V3.pdf (github.com/aifoundry-org/et-man); TI's and ADI's product pages give no device structure

tb.strap.statement: A strap (boot-option) pin: a resistor pulls the pin up to the I/O supply, and a switch can tie it to ground instead; the chip's input receiver (often a Schmitt trigger, an inverter with hysteresis, so that a slow or noisy edge gives one clean change) reads its level, and a flip-flop holds it when the chip comes out of reset.
tb.strap.source: P. Horowitz and W. Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 2015)

card.dip.statement: The card has DIP switches to set all its boot options.
card.dip.source: Esperanto, "PCIe Dev Card (V3)", ET-PCIe-Dev-Card-V3.pdf (github.com/aifoundry-org/et-man), p. 1 (features) and p. 3 (DIP switches)

et.bootpins.statement: The chip records the state of its boot pins: bits 10:0 of the reset manager's status register rm_status2 "provide status information about various boot pins": 11 bits.
et.bootpins.source: Esperanto, ET Programmer's Reference Manual (github.com/aifoundry-org/et-man), §15.2.3.18 (SPIO CRU address space), pdf p. 431

p.cu.1.statement: A copper atom has 29 electrons: 2, 8, 18 and 1 in its four shells (ground state [Ar] 3d10 4s1); pulling the one outer electron off a lone atom takes 7.726 eV.
p.cu.1.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, ground states and ionization energies (Cu I)

p.cu.2.statement: Natural copper is 69.15% copper-63 (29 protons, 34 neutrons) and 30.85% copper-65 (29 protons, 36 neutrons); its standard atomic weight is 63.546.
p.cu.2.source: NIST, Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions (Cu)

cu.free.statement: In the metal each copper atom gives its one outer electron to a shared sea: 4 atoms per 0.3615 nm cube make 8.47 x 10^28 free electrons per cubic metre, which carry the current, while the atoms stay put.
cu.free.source: arithmetic on wire.cu (the face-centred cubic cell, 0.3615 nm); one conduction electron per atom: C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (Wiley, 2005), ch. 6
cu.free.note: 4 / (0.3615e-9 m)^3 = 4 / 4.724e-29 m^3 = 8.47e28 per m^3 (Kittel lists 8.47e22 per cm^3 for copper)

size.p.cu.statement: One copper atom takes about 0.256 nm in the metal: the distance between neighbours, 0.3615 nm / sqrt(2).
size.p.cu.source: arithmetic on wire.cu (the face-centred cubic cell, 0.3615 nm)

host.intel14.statement: Intel's 14 nm process, the host processors', is a FinFET process too: fins 42 nm apart, gates 70 nm apart and the finest wires 52 nm apart (TSMC N7: 30, 57 and 40 nm).
host.intel14.source: S. Natarajan et al., "A 14nm Logic Technology Featuring 2nd-Generation FinFET, Air-Gapped Interconnects, Self-Aligned Double Patterning and a 0.0588 µm² SRAM cell size", IEDM 2014; out.host.5 (the hosts' 14 nm)

host.ddr4.statement: The hosts' processors (Core i7-11700K, i5-11600) take DDR4 memory, up to DDR4-3200 on two channels: DRAM, the same kind of one-transistor, one-capacitor cell as the card's LPDDR4X.
host.ddr4.source: Intel, Core i7-11700K and Core i5-11600 specifications (ark.intel.com: memory types up to DDR4-3200, 2 channels); the cell: ml:dram:gen.cell

size.lib.nor2.statement: NOR gate: about 240 nm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.nor2.note: about 3 gate pitches (171 nm) wide in a 240 nm-tall N7 cell, like the NAND; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.aoi21.statement: AND-OR-INVERT gate: about 300 nm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.aoi21.note: about 4 gate pitches wide (inference); an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.shifter.statement: Shifter (stages of multiplexers): about 20 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.shifter.note: a 64-bit shifter is 6 rows of 64 multiplexers, each about 0.3 µm wide; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.lzd.statement: A leading-zero counter: about 5 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.lzd.note: a 64-bit counter is about 60 small cells in six levels; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.decoder.statement: Decoder: about 3 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.decoder.note: a 7-to-128 row decoder spans the 128 rows of an array, a few µm; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.regfile.statement: Register file: about 40 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.regfile.note: like the core's integer register file: 4,096 latch bits with their ports; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.logic.statement: Control logic: standard cells: about 20 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.logic.note: a control block of a few thousand cells at 0.1-0.3 µm² each; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.counter.statement: Counter: about 3 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.counter.note: an 8- to 40-bit counter: a few dozen cells; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.cmpeq.statement: Equality comparator: about 2 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.cmpeq.note: a 23-bit comparator: 23 XNORs and a small tree; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.fifo.statement: Queue (first in, first out): about 20 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.fifo.note: a few entries of a cache line or a request, with their pointers; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.pll.statement: A phase-locked loop (PLL): about 100 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.pll.note: on the order of 100 µm across, like the shire's clock generation (size.shire.clock); an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.ecc.statement: Error correction (SECDED): about 10 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.ecc.note: the XOR trees of a 72-bit code: a few hundred gates; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.rom.statement: A read-only memory (ROM): about 20 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.rom.note: a small table of coefficients: a few thousand bits; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.diffamp.statement: A differential amplifier: about 1 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.diffamp.note: a few transistors of several fins each, sized for matching (inference); an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.xbar.statement: A crossbar switch: about 100 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.xbar.note: like the router's 8 x 8 switch of 512-bit datapaths (size.shire.meshstop.router.xbar); an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.round.statement: Rounding: about 5 µm across, the width of the view that frames it (an order of magnitude).
size.lib.round.note: a sticky OR, a compound gate and a 24-bit incrementer: a few hundred cells; an order of magnitude only: no layout of the ET-SoC-1's circuits is published.

size.lib.wire.view.statement: Copper wiring, in section: about 300 nm across, the width of the view that frames it (seven wires at the 40 nm pitch of M0-M4).
size.lib.wire.view.source: arithmetic on n7.mmp (7.5 pitches of 40 nm)
size.lib.wire.view.note: the drawing's heights are not to scale: the stack's are not published

size.lib.buck.statement: A buck converter (a switching regulator): about 2.0 cm across, the width of the view that frames it.
size.lib.buck.note: about the size of the card's regulator modules: the TPSM831D31 is 15 x 48 mm (card.tpsm), the LTM4680 16 x 16 mm (card.ltm)

size.lib.powerfet.statement: A power transistor, in section: about 5 µm across, the width of the view that frames it.
size.lib.powerfet.note: a few cells of a trench MOSFET, each a micrometre or two wide (tb.powerfet); order of magnitude only, the regulators' own devices are not published

size.lib.strap.statement: A boot switch and its pin: about 2.0 cm across, the width of the view that frames it.
size.lib.strap.note: a block of DIP switches is about 2 cm long on the card's photo (out.card.1 gives the card's 167.6 mm width); the pin and its receiver are far smaller

el.rails.statement: In CMOS logic a 0 is the ground rail, 0 V, and a 1 is the supply rail: here 0.517 V on a minion at 600 MHz. A gate at 0 V turns an n-type transistor off; a gate at the rail turns it on.
el.rails.source: C. Hu, Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits (Pearson 2010), ch. 6 (author's free chapter); the minion rail measured on this chip (et.v-minion)

el.off-channel.statement: An "off" transistor still lets about 10 billion electrons a second through, but each crosses its 16.5 nm channel in about 0.2 ps, so at any instant its channel holds on average 0.002 electrons.
el.off-channel.source: arithmetic on et.leak-per-tr (10 billion electrons a second) and si.mobility (0.2 ps to cross the channel)
el.off-channel.note: 10^10 per second x 0.2 x 10^-12 s = 0.002. An average over every transistor on the chip; a given off transistor leaks more or less.

el.half-energy.statement: At the minion rail's 0.517 V each switch costs (0.517 / 0.75)² = 0.48 of what it would at N7's nominal 0.75 V: half the energy, since the energy goes as the voltage squared.
el.half-energy.source: arithmetic on et.v-minion, et.nominal-075 and el.dynamic (E = C V²)

el.sram-electrons.statement: A 6T SRAM bit holds roughly a thousand electrons (440-1,300) on its storage node at the 0.705 V SRAM rail; a latch bit of the minion's L1 at 0.517 V holds about 320-970.
el.sram-electrons.source: arithmetic on gate.cap-fin, n7.sram-dims, et.v-sram and et.v-minion (el.sram-node)
el.sram-electrons.note: No N7 storage-node capacitance is published: 0.1-0.3 fF is assumed (el.sram-node). The inverters restore the charge all the time, so it needs no refresh.

size.p.nucleus.statement: The silicon-28 nucleus is about 8.1 fm across: a uniform sphere with its measured rms charge radius of 3.1224 fm has a radius of 4.03 fm. (The rule R = 1.2 fm x 28^(1/3) gives 7.3 fm across; a nucleus has a soft edge, so any size is a convention.)
size.p.nucleus.source: arithmetic on p.nucleus.3 (the measured rms charge radius) and p.nucleus.2 (the 1.2 A^(1/3) rule)

size.p.atom.statement: One silicon atom takes about 0.235 nm in the crystal: the distance between neighbours, sqrt(3)/4 x 0.5431 nm.
size.p.atom.note: the distance between neighbouring atoms in the crystal, sqrt(3)/4 x a = 0.2352 nm (a from CODATA 2022); each atom's share is a sphere of radius 117.6 pm. Measured covalent radius 111 pm (Cordero 2008).

size.lib.dramcell.statement: A DRAM cell of the 2019-2022 generations is roughly 0.1 µm across (an order of magnitude: about 6 F² at a feature size of 15-20 nm); the card's DRAM generation is not known.
size.lib.dramcell.source: the memory levels' DRAM cell (dram.cell, inside.json); TechInsights, DRAM scaling trend (el.dram-cell)
size.lib.dramcell.note: Order of magnitude only: the cell is about 6 F², F the half-pitch of its generation; its capacitor is far taller than it is wide.

ring.mid.statement: On a logarithmic scale the middle of all sizes, between the Planck length (1.6 x 10^-35 m) and the observable universe (8.7 x 10^26 m), is 0.12 mm: about a minion's L1 data cache.
ring.mid.source: arithmetic on p.planck.1 and the observable universe's diameter (out.universe.2): the square root of their product (p.wrap.7)
